title: Where Fatal Crashes Concentrate on Bangkok’s Major Roads
text:
The question

12,762 road deaths were recorded in Thailand between January and September 2024, 1,486 of them in the six provinces of the Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR).
A crash can only happen on a road, so I measure intensity per km of road and distance along the road, using the network methods of spNetwork.



Where on the major road network do fatal crashes concentrate?
Do they cluster along the road, and at what distance?
Do crashes close together on the road also happen close together in time?

title: Where Fatal Crashes Concentrate on Bangkok’s Major Roads
section: Data quality decides what the map can show
text:
Data quality decides what the map can show



36%


of BMR deaths have crash coordinates


16 of 586


deaths with no recorded vehicle are geocoded


97.1%


of geocoded deaths are motorcyclists



Deaths with no recorded vehicle also lack the sub-district and home province, and 91.1% carry the ICD-10 code V89.2. They most likely come from a record source without crash details.
The file needed four silent fixes, swapped latitude and longitude, Buddhist Era dates that fail on 29 February, deaths merged into crash events and OSM roads split at junctions.


The maps describe fatal motorcycle crashes with a recorded location on major roads, which is 374 of the 515 geocoded crash events.

title: Where Fatal Crashes Concentrate on Bangkok’s Major Roads
section: Half of the intensity sits on 3.1% of the road length
text:
Half of the intensity sits on 3.1% of the road length













The densest cluster is in central Bangkok, with shorter hotspots along corridors in Pathum Thani and Samut Prakan.
49% of the top 5% of road segments are in Bangkok, and 73% are primary or secondary roads.
The hotspots stay in place at 500 m (overlap 89.8%) and spread out at 2 km.


The simple method loses about 27% of the kernel mass, more near the boundary, so values are relative.

title: Where Fatal Crashes Concentrate on Bangkok’s Major Roads
section: Per km of road, primary roads and Samut Prakan stand out
text:
Per km of road, primary roads and Samut Prakan stand out













Primary and secondary roads have the highest rates under both ways of counting divided roads.
Bangkok has the most crashes, but Samut Prakan has more per km of major road.
Samut Prakan is geocoded less often than Bangkok, so geocoding bias does not explain its higher rate.


Rates are per km of road. Without traffic volumes they do not measure risk per trip.

title: Where Fatal Crashes Concentrate on Bangkok’s Major Roads
section: Weekends and the start of the year are worse
text:
Weekends and the start of the year are worse























The weekend daily rate is 1.42 times the weekday rate (chi-square p = 0.0029). Crashes peak in Jan and drift down through the year, with the same shape in the geocoded subset and in all deaths.

title: Where Fatal Crashes Concentrate on Bangkok’s Major Roads
section: Crashes cluster within about 400 m along the road
text:
Crashes cluster within about 400 m along the road


The K-function is above the random-placement envelope at 61 of 61 distances, and the G-function is above it in 8 of the 9 rings up to 400 m.


Random placement treats every km of road as equal, so part of this excess reflects uneven intensity along roads.

title: Where Fatal Crashes Concentrate on Bangkok’s Major Roads
section: Nearby crashes do not bunch in time
text:
Nearby crashes do not bunch in time













The Knox test shuffles dates among crash events and counts pairs close in both network distance and time.
Every cell has fewer close pairs than expected (ratios 0.37 to 0.91), and the smallest one-sided p-value is 0.675.


Crashes near each other on the road are spread over the months, which fits persistent crash sites and argues against short bursts.

title: Where Fatal Crashes Concentrate on Bangkok’s Major Roads
text:
Implications and limits


What the evidence supports

Target road audits, enforcement and ambulance coverage at a short list of stretches, since half of the intensity sits on 3.1% of the road length.
Allocate by crashes per km of road as well as by counts, which shifts attention to Samut Prakan and arterial roads.
Favour engineering at persistent sites over patrols after each crash.
Strengthen weekend enforcement, and focus on motorcyclists.


Where the evidence stops

Only 36% of BMR deaths have a location, and a quarter of geocoded crashes lie away from major roads.
Without traffic volumes, rates per km do not measure risk.
Random placement on the network ignores uneven intensity, so clustering mixes both effects.
Death dates stand in for crash dates.
Linking death records to police records would close the largest data gap.

title: Geospatial Analytics and Applications
text:
Meng Tingyu


Master of IT in Business, Singapore Management University
This is where I keep my work for Geospatial Analytics and Applications. Over the term it will fill up with weekly exercises and three larger take-home analyses, covering geospatial data wrangling, thematic mapping, spatial point patterns, spatial autocorrelation, clustering, and geographically weighted models.
Everything here is written in R and Quarto, and the code that produced each figure is visible on the page. I work this way for a practical reason. When an analysis is written up properly, I find out fairly quickly whether I understand the method or only know which function to call, and that gap is much cheaper to discover here than in an exam.
A word on what I am aiming for. Geospatial work makes it unusually easy to produce something that looks convincing and is quietly wrong. A map with the wrong projection still renders. A spatial weights matrix built on the wrong neighbour definition still returns a Moran’s I. So alongside the results, I try to record the assumptions each method needs and the checks I ran before trusting the output.

title: Geospatial Analytics and Applications
text:
Hands-on Exercises

Weekly guided exercises. The goal is to get the mechanics right: reading data correctly, projecting it correctly, and producing a map that is not misleading.



Hands-on Ex01
Geospatial data wrangling with sf and choropleth mapping with tmap. Projections, geoprocessing, and how much a classification scheme changes the story.


Hands-on Ex02
Spatial point patterns with spatstat. Nearest neighbour tests, kernel density, the G, F, K and L functions, and why the null hypothesis is the hard part.


Hands-on Ex03
Forest fires in Bangka Belitung across 2023. Spatio-temporal KDE with sparr, the space-time K function with stpp, and what a bootstrap says about bandwidths chosen by rule of thumb.


Hands-on Ex04
Contiguity, distance and k nearest neighbour weights for Hunan’s counties, and four ways to compute a spatial lag of GDP per capita.


Hands-on Ex05
Moran’s I, Geary’s C and correlograms for Hunan’s GDP per capita, then LISA clusters and Gi* hot and cold spots.


Hands-on Ex06
ICT regions for Shan State’s 55 townships. Ward clustering first, then SKATER and ClustGeo to see how much homogeneity it costs to keep each region in one piece.


Hands-on Ex07
Accessibility to eldercare centres across 3,125 hexagons in Singapore. Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM computed from a road distance matrix, then compared by planning region after fixing duplicated hexagons in the spatial join.


Hands-on Ex08
Huff model trade areas for 28 fast-food stores across 617 villages in Taichung.


Hands-on Ex09
Hedonic pricing of 1,436 condominium resales in Singapore. An OLS model with full diagnostics, then fixed and adaptive bandwidth GWR, and a check of where the local coefficients can be trusted.

title: Geospatial Analytics and Applications
text:
In-class Exercises

Extensions of the hands-on work into interpretation. Less about getting the code to run, more about deciding what the output actually means.



In-class Ex04
Geographically weighted summary statistics for GDP per capita in Hunan. Choosing an adaptive bandwidth by cross-validation and AICc, then mapping local means to see where the county-level picture differs from the provincial average.


In-class Ex06
Emerging hot spot analysis of GDP per capita in Hunan. A spacetime cube of county values by year, Gi* computed for each year, and the Mann-Kendall test to separate clusters that are intensifying from those that are fading.


In-class Ex07


In-class Ex08
Market area analysis with the Huff model. Village population and the distance from each village to each store give patronage probabilities, which I use to map the trade area of one store, estimate store sales against actual sales, and assign every village to its most likely store.

title: Geospatial Analytics and Applications
text:
Take-home Exercises

The larger pieces of work, where I take a real dataset and carry an analysis from raw files through to a conclusion someone could act on.



Take-home Ex01
Fatal road crashes in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region in 2024, analysed along the OpenStreetMap road network. Network kernel density, network K and G functions, and a Knox test on network distance to tell persistent crash sites from short bursts. The executive summary gives the main findings in ten slides.


Take-home Ex02
Armed conflict across Myanmar’s 330 townships from 2021 to 2025, using ACLED events. Local Moran’s I and Gi* for hot spots and outliers, emerging hot spot analysis over 19 quarters, and a bivariate LISA to find violence away from the front line. Technical report · Executive summary · GitHub

title: Hands-on Ex08: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
This exercise estimates where the customers of a fast-food franchise in Taichung City come from. I play the role of an analyst in the business development team, and the job is to map the trade area of each of the 28 existing stores.
The tool is the Huff model. For every village and every store it gives a probability that a resident of the village visits that store. The probability goes up with the attractiveness of the store and goes down with distance and with the number of competing stores nearby. The MCI package computes it with huff.shares().
The work has six parts. Part 1 and Part 2 import and clean the data. Part 3 and Part 4 build the distance matrix and the interaction matrix that MCI expects. Part 5 runs the Huff model, maps the trade area of one store and compares the estimated sales with the real sales. Part 6 adds seven checks and alternatives of my own.

Setting up

The data
The course page says four datasets are used, but the code reads five, three spatial layers and two tables. All three layers are ESRI shapefiles in TWD97 / TM2 zone 121 (EPSG 3826).








Dataset
Type
What it holds




STORES_TC
point shapefile
28 store locations with name, address and store code


TOWN_TC
polygon shapefile
28 district boundaries of Taichung City


VILLAGE_TC
polygon shapefile
622 village (里) boundaries


pop2019.csv
csv
2019 village population, H_CNT households, P_CNT total, M_CNT male, F_CNT female


Store_sales_data.csv
csv
5,499 rows of bills and sales amount by store code



The data folder also has two files the course page never uses. STORES_TC1 is a copy of the store layer with a 29th point called “New Store”, and storeCD.csv lists a Capacity of 50 for every store. I use STORES_TC1 in Section 6.7 to test what happens when a new store opens.






NoteData folder housekeeping



The download came with QGIS metadata files named STORES_TC1.qmd, TOWN_TC.qmd and VILLAGE_TC.qmd. They are XML files that only share the .qmd extension with Quarto documents, so quarto render tries to render them as pages and fails. I deleted them from data/geospatial before rendering the site.




Packages
Five packages come from the course page. I added patchwork to put maps side by side and ggrepel to label stores on scatter plots without overlap.

title: Hands-on Ex08: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
Part 2 Preparing the data

2.1 Aggregating store sales
The sales table has one row per store and POD code, so I sum it up to one row per store.


Show the code
store_sales_aggre <- store_sales %>%
  group_by(`Store Code`) %>%
  summarise(
    "Total_Bill" = sum(Bills, na.rm = TRUE),
    "Total_Sales" = sum(Amount, na.rm = TRUE))




2.2 Relational join
left_join() attaches the totals to the store layer. The same step creates Store_size, which the Huff model uses as attractiveness.


Show the code
stores <- stores %>%
  left_join(store_sales_aggre,
            by = join_by(
              Store_CD == `Store Code`)) %>%
  mutate(Store_size = 100)

summary(stores)

title: Hands-on Ex08: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
Part 3 Computing the distance matrix
Each village is reduced to one point, and the distance from that point to every store becomes the distance in the model. The course text says centroid, but the code uses st_point_on_surface(), which returns a point that is always inside the polygon.


Show the code
village_center <- st_point_on_surface(village)
distmat <- st_distance(village_center, stores)








TipWhy point on surface beats the centroid here



I checked how many true centroids fall outside their own village.


Show the code
village_cent <- st_centroid(village)
outside <- !sapply(seq_len(nrow(village)), function(i)
  st_within(village_cent[i, ], village[i, ], sparse = FALSE)[1, 1])
sum(outside)


[1] 8


Eight villages have a centroid outside their own boundary, three of them in Xitun. For these villages the centroid can sit closer to a different store, and when I reran the model with centroids the probability for one store in one village changed by up to 0.40. The store totals moved by at most 5.3%, so the effect is local, but the point on surface version is the safer choice.


The matrix is 617 by 28. To feed MCI it has to become a long table with one row per village and store pair.


Show the code
rownames(distmat) <- village$VILLCODE
colnames(distmat) <- stores$Store_CD

distmat_long <- distmat %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "VILLCODE") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -VILLCODE,
    names_to = "Store_CD",
    values_to = "distance") %>%
  mutate(distance = as.numeric(distance))

title: Hands-on Ex08: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
Part 4 Preparing the interaction matrix
MCI needs one table with origin, destination, attractiveness and distance. I add Store_size from the store layer and move distance to the last column.


Show the code
interaction_matrix <- distmat_long %>%
  left_join(
    stores %>%
      st_drop_geometry() %>%
      select(Store_CD, Store_size),
    by = "Store_CD") %>%
  relocate(distance, .after = last_col())

summary(interaction_matrix)


   VILLCODE           Store_CD           Store_size     distance      
 Length:17276       Length:17276       Min.   :100   Min.   :  108.5  
 Class :character   Class :character   1st Qu.:100   1st Qu.: 6678.7  
 Mode  :character   Mode  :character   Median :100   Median :11965.3  
                                       Mean   :100   Mean   :12762.7  
                                       3rd Qu.:100   3rd Qu.:18122.3  
                                       Max.   :100   Max.   :41395.4  


The table has 17,276 rows, which is 617 villages times 28 stores. The shortest distance is 108 m and the longest is 41.4 km, with a median of about 12 km.

title: Hands-on Ex08: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
Part 5 Computing the Huff model


Show the code
huff_share <- huff.shares(
  interaction_matrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
  "Store_size", "distance")








NoteWhat huff.shares() does with its defaults



The call does not set gamma or lambda, so MCI uses its defaults, gamma = 1 and lambda = -2 with power functions for both. Each village and store pair gets a utility of Store_size^1 × distance^-2, and p_ij is that utility divided by the sum over all 28 stores for the same village. With equal store sizes this reduces to inverse distance squared, and the 28 probabilities of every village add up to 1. Section 6.5 tests other values of lambda.



5.1 Trade area of a single store
The course text says it picks store TG, but the code filters BT. I follow the code here and map TG separately in Section 6.2.


Show the code
market_share <- huff_share %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")

Trade_area <- village %>%
  left_join(market_share, by = "VILLCODE")

selected_store <- stores %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")








WarningFixes to the course map code



I changed three things in the course code. The left_join() that builds Trade_area now names by = "VILLCODE" so the join key is explicit. tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) came after the store layer, so it drew borders on a single point and its argument did nothing in tmap v4.4. I replaced it with a district border layer from town, which also helps to read the map. Last, tm_dots() has no col argument in v4, so I switched to tm_symbols() with shape 21 to get a red dot with a black outline.




Show the code
tm_shape(Trade_area) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ij",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Patronage Probability"),
              col = "grey85",
              lwd = 0.3) +
tm_shape(town) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey35", lwd = 0.8) +
tm_shape(selected_store) +
  tm_symbols(fill = "red", col = "black",
             shape = 21, size = 0.6) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Patronage Probability of Store BT by village") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)









BT sits in Beitun District and draws most strongly from its own neighbourhood. Nine villages have a probability above 0.5 and all nine are in Beitun, led by Pingshun at 0.94, only 209 m from the store. The share drops fast once another store is closer than BT. DT is only 1.5 km away, and the villages between the two split their custom.
The map also shows something less obvious. The large rural villages in Taiping and Xinshe in the east fall in the top classes too, even though BT gets a median of only 3% to 4% there. These villages are far from every store, so the probabilities flatten out and BT ends up with a slightly bigger slice than in most of the city. Quantile classes put the same number of villages in each colour, which stretches these small values across the darker half of the legend. Section 6.1 redraws the map with fixed breaks.


5.2 Store sales analysis
The Huff model can also estimate how many customers each store should get. P_CNT from the village layer joins onto huff_share, and shares.total() multiplies each probability by the village population and sums it by store.


Show the code
huff_share_pp <- huff_share %>%
  left_join(village %>%
              st_drop_geometry() %>%
              select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
            by = "VILLCODE") %>%
  relocate(distance, .after = last_col())

huff_total <- shares.total(
  huff_share_pp, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
  "p_ij", "P_CNT")

store_sales_est <- stores %>%
  left_join(huff_total,
            by = join_by("Store_CD" == "suppliers_single"))


sum_E_j is measured in people. The 28 values add up to 2,804,359, the total population, because every resident is shared out among the stores. The comparison below is between expected customers and actual sales in dollars, so only the shape of the relationship matters.


Show the code
store_sales_nongeom <- store_sales_est %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

ggscatterstats(
  store_sales_nongeom,
  x = sum_E_j,
  y = Total_Sales)









The Pearson correlation is 0.58 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.78, t(26) = 3.60, p = 0.001). Stores with more expected customers do sell more, but a straight line explains only about a third of the variation in sales. BT gets the highest estimate at 138,306 people and ranks 15th in real sales. FH is the top seller and sits fourth in the estimate.


5.3 Reshaping to a wide table
The last chunk of the course page turns huff_share into a wide table with one row per village and one column per store.


Show the code
huff_share_wider <- huff_share %>%
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD,
              values_from = p_ij)

dim(huff_share_wider)


[1] 617  29


The course does not use it further. I use it in Section 6.3 and Section 6.4 to find the leading store in each village and how contested each village is.

title: Hands-on Ex08: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
Part 6 Going further

6.1 The same store with fixed breaks
Quantile classes answer “which villages rank highest for BT”, but they hide how large the probability is. The top decile alone covers values from 0.068 to 0.944. Fixed breaks tied to business meaning are easier to read.


Show the code
tm_shape(Trade_area) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ij",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1),
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Patronage Probability"),
              col = "grey85",
              lwd = 0.3) +
tm_shape(town) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey35", lwd = 0.8) +
tm_shape(selected_store) +
  tm_symbols(fill = "red", col = "black",
             shape = 21, size = 0.6) +
  tm_title("Store BT with fixed breaks") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_scalebar()











Show the code
table(cut(market_share$p_ij,
          breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1)))



  (0,0.05] (0.05,0.1]  (0.1,0.2]  (0.2,0.5]    (0.5,1] 
       528         45         19         16          9 


With fixed breaks the picture is much tighter. 528 of the 617 villages give BT less than 5%, and only 25 give it more than 20%. Most of the eastern villages that looked strong on the quantile map now sit in the lightest class with the rest of the city. For the business team I would show this version, since a colour then means the same probability everywhere.


6.2 Trade area of TG, the store the text meant
TG is the store in Dajia District at the north end of the network. Its nearest neighbour is 11.4 km away, the most isolated position among the 28 stores. I expected its trade area to look very different from BT’s.


Show the code
Trade_area_tg <- village %>%
  left_join(huff_share %>% filter(Store_CD == "TG"),
            by = "VILLCODE")

tm_shape(Trade_area_tg) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ij",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1),
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Patronage Probability"),
              col = "grey85",
              lwd = 0.3) +
tm_shape(town) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey35", lwd = 0.8) +
tm_shape(stores %>% filter(Store_CD == "TG")) +
  tm_symbols(fill = "red", col = "black",
             shape = 21, size = 0.6) +
  tm_title("Store TG with fixed breaks") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_scalebar()











Show the code
nn_dist <- st_distance(stores)
diag(nn_dist) <- NA
tibble(Store_CD = stores$Store_CD,
       nearest_store_m = round(apply(nn_dist, 1, min, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  arrange(desc(nearest_store_m)) %>%
  head(5)


# A tibble: 5 × 2
  Store_CD nearest_store_m
  <chr>              <dbl>
1 TG                 11423
2 EH                 11055
3 OL                  6156
4 TZ                  4272
5 ET                  4257


Show the code
table(cut(Trade_area_tg$p_ij,
          breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1)))



  (0,0.05] (0.05,0.1]  (0.1,0.2]  (0.2,0.5]    (0.5,1] 
       542         14          8         24         29 


TG holds more than half the custom in 29 villages, against 9 for BT. Twenty of them are in Dajia, seven in Daan and two in Waipu, and the highest value reaches 0.99. With no store nearby, the model hands TG almost the whole northern coast. Yet TG has the second lowest real sales of the 28 stores, which already hints that distance alone does not explain sales well. Section 6.6 looks at this.


6.3 Primary trade areas from the wide table
The Huff probabilities overlap, so every store has some share everywhere. A common way to draw clean boundaries is to give each village to the store with the highest probability. The wide table makes this a one-liner with max.col().


Show the code
p_mat <- as.matrix(huff_share_wider[, -1])

dominant <- tibble(
  VILLCODE  = huff_share_wider$VILLCODE,
  dom_store = colnames(p_mat)[max.col(p_mat, ties.method = "first")],
  max_p     = apply(p_mat, 1, max),
  eff_n     = 1 / rowSums(p_mat^2))

primary_area <- village %>%
  left_join(dominant, by = "VILLCODE") %>%
  group_by(dom_store) %>%
  summarise(n_village = n(),
            population = sum(P_CNT))




Show the code
tm_shape(primary_area) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "dom_store",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                values = "brewer.set3"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend_hide(),
              col = "white",
              lwd = 1.2) +
tm_shape(stores) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3) +
  tm_labels(text = "Store_CD", size = 0.6) +
  tm_title("Primary trade area of each store") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE)









The map splits Taichung into 28 cells, one per store. The cells are small and tightly packed in the central districts and become very large toward the edges, where TG, EH and WF each cover a huge rural area.


Show the code
primary_area %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(desc(population))


# A tibble: 28 × 3
   dom_store n_village population
   <chr>         <int>      <dbl>
 1 FY               36     157239
 2 SA               40     155947
 3 DD               30     148393
 4 BT               23     134771
 5 JW               23     131763
 6 TG               54     131499
 7 FH               38     131410
 8 DT               20     119962

10 ZS               25     112485
# ℹ 18 more rows


Show the code
nearest <- huff_share %>%
  group_by(VILLCODE) %>%
  slice_min(distance, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup()
mean(nearest$Store_CD ==
       dominant$dom_store[match(nearest$VILLCODE, dominant$VILLCODE)])


[1] 1


Every store leads in at least nine villages, so no store is fully shadowed by its neighbours. FY has the largest primary population at 157,239 and LM the smallest at 57,631. The last line returns 1, which means the leading store is always the nearest store. With equal attractiveness this map is simply a Thiessen (Voronoi) partition clipped to the villages. A real size or brand variable would be needed before this map says anything more than the distance map does.


6.4 How contested each village is
The highest probability in a village tells me how loyal that village is to one store. A value near 1 means one store dominates, and a value near 0.1 means the custom is spread thin. I also computed the effective number of stores, 1 / sum(p^2), which reads as “how many equally strong stores this village behaves as if it had”.


Show the code
contest <- village %>%
  left_join(dominant, by = "VILLCODE")

tm_shape(contest) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "max_p",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1),
                values = "brewer.yl_gn_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Highest store probability"),
              col = NA) +
tm_shape(town) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.6) +
tm_shape(stores) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.2, fill = "black") +
  tm_title("How strongly the leading store holds each village") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE)











Show the code
summary(dominant$max_p)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
0.07467 0.26862 0.41240 0.47527 0.65404 0.99603 


Show the code
sum(dominant$max_p < 0.3)


[1] 191


Show the code
town_lookup <- town %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(TOWNCODE, TOWNENG)

contest %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%

The map shows dark rings around each store and pale gaps in between. In 191 villages, close to a third, no store reaches 30%. The most contested districts are Dadu (mean highest probability 0.23, about 13.7 effective stores), Qingshui (0.29) and Xinshe (0.31), and none of the three has a store of its own. 6.5 Tuning the distance decay
The default lambda = -2 is a textbook value and was never fitted to this data. I reran the model with a range of decay values and checked which one tracks the real sales best. The real huff.shares() loops over every row and is slow, so I wrote a short vectorised version and first confirmed it gives the same answer.


Show the code
huff_fast <- function(im, lambda = -2, gamma = 1) {
  im %>%
    group_by(VILLCODE) %>%
    mutate(U_ij = Store_size^gamma * distance^lambda,
           p_ij = U_ij / sum(U_ij)) %>%
    ungroup()
}

check <- huff_fast(interaction_matrix) %>%
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_fast = p_ij) %>%
  left_join(huff_share %>% select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij),
            by = c("VILLCODE", "Store_CD"))
all.equal(check$p_fast, check$p_ij)


[1] TRUE




Show the code
pop_lookup <- village %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(VILLCODE, P_CNT)

lambda_fit <- map_dfr(seq(-0.5, -4, by = -0.25), function(l) {
  est <- huff_fast(interaction_matrix, lambda = l) %>%
    left_join(pop_lookup, by = "VILLCODE") %>%
    group_by(Store_CD) %>%
    summarise(E_j = sum(p_ij * P_CNT)) %>%
    left_join(store_sales_nongeom %>% select(Store_CD, Total_Sales),
              by = "Store_CD")
  tibble(lambda = l,
         pearson = cor(est$E_j, est$Total_Sales),
         spearman = cor(est$E_j, est$Total_Sales, method = "spearman"))
})

lambda_fit %>%
  pivot_longer(-lambda, names_to = "measure", values_to = "r") %>%
  ggplot(aes(lambda, r, colour = measure)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -2, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_colour_discrete(labels = c(pearson = "Pearson",
                                   spearman = "Spearman")) +
  labs(x = "lambda (distance decay)",
       y = "Correlation with actual sales",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Weaker distance decay tracks real sales better") +
  theme_minimal()









The correlation falls steadily as the decay gets stronger. It is 0.67 at lambda = -0.5, 0.58 at the default of -2 and 0.32 at -4, and the Spearman curve follows the same path. A weaker decay means customers are less put off by distance than the default assumes, which fits a city where people drive or ride scooters to eat. I also tried an exponential decay and got 0.68 at a rate of 0.1 per km, about the same as the best power value.
I would not pick a new lambda from this alone. With only 28 stores, 0.67 and 0.58 both sit inside each other’s confidence interval. The proper way is to calibrate on where customers actually live. The sales file has a POD code per row that looks like a customer zone, but there is no lookup from those codes to villages, so I could not use it.


6.6 Which stores sell more or less than expected
I fitted a simple linear model of sales on expected customers and looked at the standardised residuals. A store far below the line sells less than its location suggests, and a store far above sells more.


Show the code

resid_tbl <- store_sales_nongeom %>%
  mutate(std_resid = rstandard(fit),
         sales_per_customer = Total_Sales / sum_E_j,
         flag = case_when(std_resid < -1 ~ "Below",
                          std_resid >  1 ~ "Above",
                          TRUE ~ "Within"))

  geom_text_repel(aes(label = Store_CD), size = 3,

  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Below = "#c0504d",

  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +

       y = "Actual sales",

title: Hands-on Ex08: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model
text:
My takeaway
The Huff model in this exercise is driven by distance alone, because every store has the same Store_size. That makes the trade area maps easy to build and also limits what they can say. The primary trade area map came out as a plain Voronoi partition, and the leading store in every one of the 617 villages was simply the nearest one.
The sales check gave a moderate fit, r = 0.58, and the residuals were more useful than the fit itself. TG, QH and ZS sell far less than their locations predict, and DD, WF and ZK sell far more. A weaker decay of -0.5 raised the fit to 0.67, but with 28 stores I treat that as a hint until it can be calibrated on where customers live.
The two classification schemes for BT showed me how much the map design changes the message. Quantile classes made BT look strong in the eastern hills where its median share is 3% to 4%, and fixed breaks showed those villages as weak.
On the data side, the five missing villages were unassigned coastal land and the eight unmatched population rows were the whole of Heping District. Neither changes the result much, but I only found them by checking what was dropped. The New Store scenario showed TY, MT and FH would lose 8% to 11% of their expected customers if NS opens in North District.

title: Hands-on Ex06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering
text:
This exercise groups the 55 townships of Shan State in Myanmar into regions with similar access to information and communication technology. The grouping uses six household ICT measures from the 2014 census, radio, television, land line phone, mobile phone, computer and internet at home.
Planners often want regions that are both homogeneous and joined together on the map. Ordinary cluster analysis only looks at the first condition. The second half of the exercise adds the map back in, first with SKATER, which cuts a minimum spanning tree of neighbouring townships, and then with ClustGeo, which lets me choose how much weight geography gets.
The work is split into six parts. Part 1 explores the variables with charts and choropleth maps, Part 2 checks correlations, and Part 3 runs hierarchical clustering. Part 4 and Part 5 cover the two spatially constrained methods, and Part 6 profiles the clusters.

Setting up

The data
Two datasets come from the Myanmar Information Management Unit (MIMU).
The first is myanmar_township_boundaries, an ESRI shapefile with the polygon boundary of every township in Myanmar. The second is Shan-ICT.csv, an extract of the 2014 Myanmar Population and Housing Census at township level. It has the number of households in each township and the number that own each of the six ICT items.
I put the shapefile in data/geospatial and the csv in data/aspatial, and added an empty data/rds folder for the intermediate files. The notes use chap12/data/..., and I changed every path to match this folder layout.


Packages


Show the code

               ggpubr, cluster, factoextra, NbClust,
               heatmaply, corrplot, psych, tidyverse, GGally)


The packages fall into five groups. sf and spdep handle the spatial data, and tidyverse covers readr, dplyr, tidyr and ggplot2 for the attribute data. tmap draws the choropleth maps. corrplot, ggpubr, heatmaply, psych and GGally are used to visualise the variables, and cluster, factoextra, NbClust and ClustGeo run the cluster analysis.






Notergdal is no longer needed



The package list in the notes mentions rgdal. It was retired from CRAN in 2023, and sf now does all of its reading and writing work, so I left it out. The p_load() call in the notes already does not include it.

Six new fields now sit at the end of the table, RADIO_PR, TV_PR, LLPHONE_PR, MPHONE_PR, COMPUTER_PR and INTERNET_PR. Television is the most common item, with a median of 517 households per thousand. Computers and home internet are rare, with medians of 19 and 23 per thousand.

title: Hands-on Ex06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering
text:
Part 1, Exploratory data analysis

Distribution of radio ownership
A histogram shows the overall shape of a variable, and a boxplot picks out outliers. I started with the raw count of households with a radio.


Show the code
ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
       aes(x=`RADIO`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")











Show the code
ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
       aes(x=`RADIO`)) +
  geom_boxplot(color="black", 
               fill="light blue")









The count is heavily right skewed, with a skewness of about 2.6. Three quarters of the townships have fewer than 6,200 radio households, and three outliers sit far to the right, Taunggyi with 30,176, Lashio with 15,307 and Nyaungshwe with 13,801. These are also among the four townships with the most households.
Next I plotted the radio penetration rate.


Show the code
ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
       aes(x=`RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")











Show the code
ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
       aes(x=`RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_boxplot(color="black", 
               fill="light blue")









The course asks what the two distributions reveal. Dividing by households removes most of the skew. RADIO_PR has a mean of 216 and a median of 211 per thousand, and its skewness drops to 0.48. The boxplot now flags only one outlier, Ywangan, where 485 of every thousand households own a radio. Taunggyi, the largest outlier in the raw counts, has a rate of 365 and sits inside the whiskers, so its earlier position came from size alone.


Distributions of all six rates
I drew one histogram for each rate and arranged them with ggarrange() from ggpubr.


Show the code
radio <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

tv <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `TV_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

llphone <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `LLPHONE_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

mphone <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `MPHONE_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

computer <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `COMPUTER_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

internet <- ggplot(data=ict_derived, 
             aes(x= `INTERNET_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")




Show the code
ggarrange(radio, tv, llphone, mphone, computer, internet, 
          ncol = 3, 
          nrow = 2)









The six rates fall into two shapes. Radio, television and mobile phone are roughly bell shaped, with television slightly skewed to the left (skewness -0.38). Land line phone, computer and internet are right skewed, with skewness between 1.3 and 1.8, because most townships have very low rates and a handful have much higher ones.


Joining the census data to the boundaries
The choropleth maps need the rates attached to the polygons. left_join() keeps shan_sf as the base, so the result is still an sf object, and adds the columns of ict_derived by matching TS_PCODE.


Show the code
shan_sf <- left_join(shan_sf, 
                     ict_derived, by=c("TS_PCODE"="TS_PCODE"))
  
write_rds(shan_sf, "data/rds/shan_sf.rds")


All 55 township codes match in both directions, so no township is dropped or left without data.






NoteWhy TS.x and TS.y appear



The notes mention a message naming the join field. With by written out there is no message. Both tables have DT, DT_PCODE and TS columns besides the key, so dplyr keeps both copies and adds the suffixes .x and .y. I checked that TS.x and TS.y hold the same township name in all 55 rows. That is why the later code refers to TS.x.




Show the code
shan_sf <- read_rds("data/rds/shan_sf.rds")




Choropleth map of the radio penetration rate
qtm() gives a quick map with default settings.


Show the code
qtm(shan_sf, "RADIO_PR")









Radio ownership is highest in the west of Shan South and Shan North. Ywangan, Pindaya and Lawksawk near Taunggyi and Mabein in the north west all exceed 380 per thousand. The lowest rates are in the north east along the Chinese border, Konkyan and Laukkaing in the Kokang area at 21 and 53, and Narphan and Pangwaun in the Wa area at about 75.


Counts versus rates on the map
To show how much the counts depend on township size, I mapped total households next to the number of radio households. The notes use tmap v3 syntax here, and I translated it to v4, where the classification goes into tm_scale_intervals().


Show the code
TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "TT_HOUSEHOLDS",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Total households")) + 
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) 

RADIO.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "RADIO",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Number Radio")) + 
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) 

tmap_arrange(TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map, RADIO.map,
             asp=NA, ncol=2)









The two maps look almost the same. Taunggyi and Lashio are in the top class on both, and the correlation between total households and radio households across the 55 townships is 0.94.
Next I put total households next to the rate. The notes do this with two variables in one tm_polygons() call and tm_facets(sync = TRUE). In v4, a vector of variables in fill already produces facets, and fill.free = TRUE gives each one its own Jenks classes.


Show the code
tm_shape(shan_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "RADIO_PR"),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks"),
              fill.free = TRUE,
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_facets(ncol = 2) +
  tm_layout(outer.margins = 0, asp = 0)















WarningTranslating the tmap v3 code



Three changes were needed for tmap 4.4. tm_fill(col = ..., n = 5, style = "jenks", title = ...) became tm_polygons(fill = ..., fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5), fill.legend = tm_legend(title = ...)). tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) became tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5), since a border is a line. tm_legend(legend.position = ...) was replaced by a position inside the fill.legend argument.


The course asks whether I can see the differences. The rate map breaks the link with size. Taunggyi, the largest township, drops to the fourth of five classes for RADIO_PR, and Lashio, the second largest, falls to the middle class at 236 per thousand. Small townships such as Mabein (8,632 households) and Monghpyak (6,165) move into the top class. The correlation between total households and RADIO_PR is only 0.34, which confirms that the rate measures something different from size.

title: Hands-on Ex06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering
text:
Part 2, Correlation analysis
Cluster analysis treats each variable as a separate dimension. Two variables that carry almost the same information would count that information twice, so I checked the correlations between the six rates first.


Show the code
cluster_vars.cor = cor(ict_derived[,12:17])
corrplot.mixed(cluster_vars.cor,
         lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black")









COMPUTER_PR and INTERNET_PR have the strongest correlation, 0.87, so I keep only one of them. Following the notes, I keep COMPUTER_PR. The next highest pairs are MPHONE_PR with COMPUTER_PR at 0.74 and TV_PR with MPHONE_PR at 0.72. They are high but well below 0.87, and the notes keep all of them.
Radio stands apart from the rest. Its correlation with the other rates ranges from -0.31 with land line phones to 0.24 with television. Radio is common in townships where the more modern items are rare, so it adds information the other variables do not have.

title: Hands-on Ex06: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering
text:
Part 3, Hierarchical cluster analysis

Extracting the clustering variables
I dropped the geometry and kept the township name with the five clustering variables.


Show the code
cluster_vars <- shan_sf %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL) %>%
  select("TS.x", "RADIO_PR", "TV_PR", "LLPHONE_PR", "MPHONE_PR", "COMPUTER_PR")
head(cluster_vars,10)

2    Pindaya 417.4647 505.1300   19.83584  162.3917    12.88190
3    Ywangan 484.5215 260.5734   11.93591  120.2856     4.41465
4   Pinlaung 231.6499 541.7189   28.54454  249.4903    13.76255

10   Kyaukme 210.9548 601.1773   39.58267  372.4930    30.94709


INTERNET_PR is left out because of its correlation with COMPUTER_PR.
The clustering functions use row names as labels, so I replaced the row numbers with township names.


Show the code
row.names(cluster_vars) <- cluster_vars$"TS.x"
head(cluster_vars,10)


               TS.x RADIO_PR    TV_PR LLPHONE_PR MPHONE_PR COMPUTER_PR
Mongmit     Mongmit 286.1852 554.1313   35.30618  260.6944    12.15939
Pindaya     Pindaya 417.4647 505.1300   19.83584  162.3917    12.88190
Ywangan     Ywangan 484.5215 260.5734   11.93591  120.2856     4.41465
Pinlaung   Pinlaung 231.6499 541.7189   28.54454  249.4903    13.76255
Mabein       Mabein 449.4903 708.6423   72.75255  392.6089    16.45042
Kalaw         Kalaw 280.7624 611.6204   42.06478  408.7951    29.63160
Pekon         Pekon 318.6118 535.8494   39.83270  214.8476    18.97032
