h = 44867.77  ; lambda = 20.17978 
Done.


Show the code
bt


          h      lambda 
45230.39047    19.05976 








WarningSet the seed, and expect this chunk to take a while



Two practical points. The routine is stochastic, so without set.seed() the optimiser lands on slightly different values every run and the numbers quoted in the prose stop matching the numbers in the output. Seeding it is not optional in a document that is meant to be reproducible.
The second point is runtime. This is a bootstrap over 905 events on a lattice with one slice per day and it took several minutes on my machine, with the optimiser printing every candidate pair as it goes. Because the site renders with freeze enabled it only pays that cost once, but it is worth knowing before assuming the render has hung.


The optimiser starts from the rule of thumb pair, throws lambda out to an enormous value on an early probe, and then works its way back down, wandering through both coordinates before settling. What it lands on is h of about 45.2 kilometres and lambda of about 19.1 days. Both are larger than the rule of thumb pair, by factors of about 2.4 in space and 3 in time.
I had expected the two to disagree in direction, and they do not. The bootstrap says the rule of thumb undersmoothed in both dimensions at once, and the spatial correction is the larger surprise, since a bandwidth of 45.2 kilometres is a substantial fraction of the width of Bangka itself. What that amounts to is a judgement about how much structure 905 events spread across a province this size can actually support. The rule of thumb was resolving features that, on a bootstrap estimate of the mean integrated squared error, are more likely to be noise than signal.

Recomputing the density


Show the code
kde_yday2 <- spattemp.density(fire_yday_owin,
                              h = round(bt[["h"]], -2),
                              lambda = round(bt[["lambda"]]))
summary(kde_yday2)


Spatiotemporal Kernel Density Estimate

Bandwidths
  h = 45200 (spatial)
  lambda = 19 (temporal)

No. of observations
  905 

Spatial bound
  Type: polygonal
  2D enclosure: [512066.8, 930756.9] x [9579205, 9834915]

Temporal bound
  [10, 360]

Evaluation
  128 x 128 x 351 trivariate lattice
  Density range: [5.296593e-16, 9.925739e-13]


The values are rounded off, to the nearest hundred metres and the nearest day, which is what the chapter does and which is reasonable given the optimiser is only accurate to within its own tolerance anyway. Carrying five significant figures on a bootstrapped bandwidth would suggest a precision that is not there.






NoteThe chapter overwrites kde_yday, I did not



The course code reassigns the result to kde_yday, which replaces the rule of thumb estimate computed in the previous section. I kept the two under separate names so that both remain in memory and the comparison below actually works. If you follow the chapter literally and then scroll back up, the earlier summary and the object no longer agree with each other, which is the kind of thing that makes a rendered document quietly inconsistent with itself.


Comparing the two summaries, the maximum density roughly halves, which is what spreading the same total mass over a wider kernel does, and the minimum rises by more than ten orders of magnitude. That second number is the more telling one. Under the narrow bandwidths the quiet parts of the year and the far corners of the province were being assigned effectively zero density, because nothing was close enough in either space or time to contribute anything at all. With the wider pair every point now borrows something from its surroundings, so the surface never collapses to nothing.


Plotting the improved estimate
The same warning about plot() applies here, since this object has the same one slice per day lattice, so I name the days again rather than letting it animate.


Show the code
par(mfcol = c(2, 3))
for (d in days) {
  plot(kde_yday2, d,
       override.par = FALSE,
       fix.range = TRUE,
       main = paste("Bootstrap KDE at day", d))
}









Set against the six panels from the previous section, the surfaces are broader and the separate cores have merged into larger regions, which is the wider spatial bandwidth doing its work, and the change from panel to panel is gentler, which is the wider temporal one. The peak sits in the same place and the same part of the year, so the substantive answer has not moved. What has changed is how much detail I am willing to believe in it, and the answer is a good deal less.


Show the code
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_yday, days[3], override.par = FALSE, fix.range = TRUE,
     main = paste("Day", days[3], "rule of thumb"))
plot(kde_yday2, days[3], override.par = FALSE, fix.range = TRUE,
     main = paste("Day", days[3], "bootstrap"))









Side by side at the same day the difference is clear enough. The left panel resolves several distinct cores with cooler ground between them, while the right panel merges them into one broad region and the outlying islands are no longer separated from the main mass. One caveat on reading this pair, fix.range holds the colour scale constant within each object across its own time slices, and it does not harmonise the scale between two different objects, so the two panels should be compared on shape and not on colour.






TipMy takeaway



Two separate lessons landed in this section of the exercise, and they point in different directions.
The first is that the gap between the monthly and the daily estimates was entirely about how I encoded time, not about the fires. Same 905 events, same locations, same spatial bandwidth, and two very different temporal resolutions purely because one version rounded every date to a month first. Aggregating a continuous variable before handing it to a smoother throws away exactly the information the smoother exists to use, and the bandwidth selector then quietly agrees that there is nothing left to smooth.
The second is that even with the time variable encoded properly, the default bandwidths were too narrow in both dimensions, and by a wide margin in space. I would not have caught that by eye, because the rule of thumb surface looked entirely plausible on its own, and if anything it looked more informative, since more structure reads as more insight. It only became visible once there was a second surface to hold it against. That is an argument for running the bootstrap as a matter of course rather than treating it as an optional refinement, and a caution against trusting a hotspot map because it has a lot of hotspots on it.

title: Hands-on Ex03: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
section: Spatio-temporal point pattern analysis with stpp
text:
Spatio-temporal point pattern analysis with stpp
Everything so far describes intensity. None of it answers the first research question, which is about independence, and for that I need a second order summary. The stpp package provides the space-time inhomogeneous K function, which compares the observed number of events within a spatial distance u and a temporal lag v against what would be expected if space and time were independent of one another.

Building the stpp object
stpp does not read sf objects, so the coordinates have to be pulled out into a plain data frame.


Show the code
coords <- st_coordinates(fire_sf)




Show the code
fire_df <- data.frame(
  x = coords[, 1],
  y = coords[, 2],
  t = fire_sf$`DayofYear`)




Show the code
fire_stpp <- as.3dpoints(fire_df)
class(fire_stpp)


[1] "stpp"








NoteThe function is as.3dpoints, with an s



The chapter text refers to as.3dpoint() in the sentence above the code chunk while the code chunk itself calls as.3dpoints(). The plural form is the one that exists. Small thing, but it cost me a minute of wondering whether the package had failed to load properly.
The other detail in that step is that t has to be an integer. This is why DayofYear is used rather than the date, and it is the same constraint that applied to the ppp marks earlier.




Show the code
plot(fire_stpp)









The default plot gives the spatial configuration alongside the temporal one, with the time dimension shown as a cumulative count. The cumulative curve is the clearest single picture of the seasonality in this whole exercise, flat until around day 180, steep from day 200 to day 300, and flat again after that.


The space-time inhomogeneous K function


Show the code
kbb_stik <- STIKhat(fire_stpp)




Show the code
plotK(kbb_stik)


The contour plot shows the estimated K function over a grid of spatial distances u on one axis and temporal lags v on the other. The version below plots the departure from the theoretical value under independence, which I find easier to read because the reference level is zero rather than a curved surface.


Show the code
plotK(kbb_stik, L = TRUE)




Reading the plot
The guide gives the rule for interpreting this, and the two cases are straightforward. High values at small u and small v mean events are occurring close together in both space and time, which is clustering. Contours that are flat or low indicate something closer to a random arrangement at those distances.
What I see here is that the values are highest in the bottom left corner of the plot, at the shortest spatial distances and the shortest temporal lags, and that they fall away as either axis increases. The contour lines are packed tightly near the origin and spread out further along, which says the clustering is concentrated at short range and decays fairly quickly rather than persisting across the whole study region and the whole year. Reading along the u axis at a fixed small v, the excess is substantial for the first part of the range and then thins out. Reading along the v axis at a fixed small u, the same shape appears, so fires that are near each other in space also tend to be near each other in time.
That is the answer to both research questions, and it is consistent with the density surfaces. The events are neither spatially nor spatio-temporally independent, and the clustering sits in southern and central Bangka during the August to October window.






ImportantThe default study region is a box, not the archipelago



This is the limitation I would flag if I were handing this analysis to anyone. When s.region is not supplied, STIKhat() falls back on a rectangle derived from the coordinates, and for an archipelago that rectangle contains a large amount of sea where a fire can never occur. Any K function estimate compares the observed pattern against what would be expected under independence within the region it thinks it is working in, so an inflated region inflates the apparent clustering.
Passing the real boundary is possible in principle, since STIKhat() accepts a two column matrix of polygon vertices, but the dissolved boundary here is 536 disconnected polygons carrying 147,452 vertices, and the function expects a single simple polygon. Simplifying it heavily with st_simplify() would be the practical route. I have not done that here because it changes the region enough that the result would no longer be comparable to the chapter’s, but the direction of the bias is clear, and I would expect the true departure from independence to be smaller than what this plot shows.
The same criticism does not apply to the sparr estimates earlier, since those were clipped to kbb_owin properly.








TipMy takeaway



The KDE surfaces and the K function are answering different questions and I had been treating them as interchangeable. A density map tells me where the events are concentrated, and it will produce a hotspot even if the process is completely random, because random patterns have lumps in them. The K function is the part that asks whether the lumps are more pronounced than randomness would produce. Ex02 made that point for the purely spatial case, and this chapter extends it to time, where the intuition is less obvious because a seasonal peak feels like it must be clustering when in fact it could just be a non-constant background rate.

title: Hands-on Ex03: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
section: Where this leaves the two questions
text:
Where this leaves the two questions
On the first question, the fire locations are not independent, either spatially or spatio-temporally. The K function sits above the independence reference across short distances and short lags, and the departure is largest where both are small.
On the second question, the clustering is concentrated on Bangka rather than Belitung, with the strongest and most persistent intensity in the central and southern parts of the island, and it is concentrated in time between roughly day 200 and day 300, which runs from the middle of July to the end of October. All three density estimates put the single most active point in the same part of September and the same part of Bangka. The bootstrap version smooths the cores together rather than relocating them, which is the reassuring outcome, since the answer would be much weaker if the position of the peak depended on the bandwidth.
The caveat attached to all of this is the region problem described above. The location and timing of the clustering are robust, since they come from the density surfaces, which were clipped to the correct window. The strength of the departure from independence is the part I would not want to quote without redoing the K function on a properly specified region.

title: Hands-on Ex03: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
section: What I would change on a second pass
text:
What I would change on a second pass
Two things. I would encode time as day of year from the beginning and run BOOT.spattemp() before drawing anything, since the monthly estimate turned out to be an artefact of aggregation and the rule of thumb estimate turned out to be undersmoothed in both dimensions, and keeping all three in the document is only worthwhile because the contrast is instructive. And I would spend the time simplifying the boundary polygon down to something STIKhat() will accept, because a second order statistic computed on the wrong region is not really a second order statistic.

title: Hands-on Exercise 01: Geospatial Data Wrangling and Choropleth Mapping
text:
This exercise covers the first two chapters of the course reference, which between them run from raw files to a finished map.
The first part is data preparation. I import vector data in three different formats, get their coordinate reference systems to agree, turn a table of latitudes and longitudes into a spatial object, and then use two small geoprocessing tasks to answer questions that are only answerable once the data is spatial.
The second part joins population figures to subzone boundaries and maps the result as a choropleth. Most of the effort there goes into the classification scheme rather than into drawing the map, because the same numbers produce very different looking maps depending on how the classes are cut.
The third part is my own. I wanted to put numbers on three things the chapters mention in passing but do not test, which are how many classes a choropleth can usefully carry, whether counting points inside a polygon boundary is a fair way to measure provision, and how much the answers move when the boundary vintage changes.






NoteReference



Chapter 1, Geospatial Data Science with R, and Chapter 2, Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R, from the course reference guide.

title: Hands-on Exercise 01: Geospatial Data Wrangling and Choropleth Mapping
text:
Getting started

pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse, classInt, units, knitr)

I use p_load() rather than a series of library() calls because it installs anything that is missing before loading it. For a document that is supposed to be reproducible on a machine other than mine, that matters more than the keystrokes it saves.
The packages break down as follows. sf handles everything geospatial, from reading files to reprojecting to geoprocessing. tmap draws the thematic maps. tidyverse brings readr for the csv files, dplyr for the joins and mutations, tidyr for reshaping the population table and ggplot2 for the statistical charts. classInt is not in the chapter, and I added it in Part 3 so that I could compute class breaks outside of tmap and inspect them directly. units keeps areas labelled with their units instead of turning them into bare numbers.

A note on tmap versions

packageVersion("tmap")

[1] '4.4'


The course materials are written against tmap version 3, and the version on my machine is version 4. Version 4 changed the argument system substantially. The old syntax still runs through a compatibility layer, but it prints deprecation notices on every map, which makes the rendered document very hard to read.
I have used version 4 syntax throughout. These are the substitutions involved.







tmap v3
tmap v4




tm_fill(col = "X", style = "quantile", palette = "Blues")
tm_polygons(fill = "X", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", values = "brewer.blues"))


tm_layout(main.title = "...")
tm_title("...")


tm_scale_bar()
tm_scalebar()


tm_polygons(col = "X")
tm_polygons(fill = "X"), since col now sets the border colour


tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)
tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)



The fourth one caught me out for a while. In version 4 col means the border colour on a polygon layer, so passing the thematic variable to col produces a map where the borders are coloured and the fills are all grey, which looks like a rendering bug rather than a syntax error.

title: Hands-on Exercise 01: Geospatial Data Wrangling and Choropleth Mapping
text:
Data provenance
The chapters name six datasets. Two of them needed a substitution, and I have recorded both rather than quietly swapping them.
The first substitution is the boundary file. Chapter 1 asks for Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web). The portal now serves the (No Sea) variant of the same 2014 boundary definition. The two differ in where the polygons stop at the coast, with (No Sea) clipped to the coastline and (Web) extending out over the water. For this exercise the clipped version is the better one anyway, because the pre-school density calculation divides by subzone area, and sea polygons would inflate the denominator without contributing any pre-schools.
The second is the file format. The portal now serves GeoJSON where the chapters expect shapefile and KML. I kept GeoJSON, and there is a section below on what I found when I tried the KML round trip, which turned out to be more instructive than simply noting that the format changed.

title: Hands-on Exercise 01: Geospatial Data Wrangling and Choropleth Mapping
text:
Part 1, geospatial data wrangling

Importing the geospatial layers

mpsz14 <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson")

z_range:       zmin: 0 zmax: 0
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84








TipReading the st_read message



The message that st_read() prints is worth actually reading rather than scrolling past, because three of the things in it will cause silent errors later if they are wrong.
The geometry type tells me which operations are meaningful. The subzones are multipolygons, the cycling paths are multilinestrings and the pre-schools are points. I can buffer a line, but asking for its area would return zero and no warning.
The bounding box is the fastest sanity check available. The values here are around 103 to 104 and 1.1 to 1.5, which are degrees of longitude and latitude. If the file had arrived in a projected system the numbers would be in the tens of thousands, because SVY21 measures metres from an origin southwest of the island.
The declared coordinate reference system is WGS84 in all three cases, which is the problem the projection section deals with.




Looking inside a simple feature data frame
An sf object is a data frame with an extra list column holding the geometries. Every dplyr verb works on it, and the geometry travels with the rows through filters and joins. Three functions give three different views of it.

st_geometry(mpsz14)

Geometry set for 323 features 
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
First 5 geometries:

$ SUBZONE_NO   <int> 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 10, 12, 4, 6, 1, 1, 3, 8, 3, 7, 9, 2, 1…

$ CA_IND       <chr> "Y", "N", "Y", "Y", "Y", "Y", "N", "Y", "N", "Y", "Y", "Y…
$ PLN_AREA_N   <chr> "OUTRAM", "BUKIT MERAH", "OUTRAM", "DOWNTOWN CORE", "DOWN…

3    4297.600 MULTIPOLYGON (((103.8438 1....


st_geometry() returns the geometry column on its own, so it shows the geometry type, the extent and the CRS while saying nothing about the attributes. glimpse() does the opposite and lists every column with its type, which is how I would notice a count field that has arrived as text. head() shows what a complete record looks like, with the attributes and the geometry side by side.


A first plot

plot(mpsz14)








The default plot of an sf object draws one small map per attribute, up to a limit. It is useful for a first look and useless for anything else, since none of the panels is large enough to read.

plot(st_geometry(mpsz14))









plot(mpsz14["PLN_AREA_N"])








Passing a single column name plots that attribute alone. Base plot() is the right tool for checking that the geometry loaded correctly, and tmap is the right tool for anything that another person is going to look at.
Now the thing the chapter asks about, which is what happens when the pre-schools are overlaid on the subzones before the projections are fixed.

plot(st_geometry(mpsz14))
plot(st_geometry(preschool), add = TRUE)














ImportantWhy the pre-schools can fail to appear



In my case both layers arrived in WGS84, so they do line up and the overlay works. In the chapter’s version the subzone layer was already in SVY21 while the pre-schools were still in WGS84, and the pre-school points landed at coordinates around 103 and 1, which read as SVY21 metres is a point roughly a hundred metres from the projection origin. That is far outside the plotting extent of the subzone layer, so the points get drawn off the edge of the canvas and nothing shows.
The failure mode is worth noting even though I did not hit it. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and the map simply comes back looking like the second layer failed to load. The same mismatch inside a distance calculation would return a number instead of an empty map, and that number would be wrong by a factor of about a hundred thousand.




Working with projection

st_crs(mpsz14)$input

[1] "WGS 84"

st_crs(cyclingpath)$input

[1] "WGS 84"

st_crs(preschool)$input

[1] "WGS 84"


All three layers are in WGS84, EPSG:4326. That is a geographic coordinate system whose units are degrees, which makes it unusable for anything involving distance or area. A buffer of five in this system would be five degrees, which is somewhere around 555 kilometres. Worse, a degree of longitude and a degree of latitude are not the same distance on the ground, so even the shape of the buffer would be wrong.
Singapore’s national projected system is SVY21, EPSG:3414, and its units are metres.

mpsz14 <- st_transform(mpsz14, crs = 3414)
cyclingpath <- st_transform(cyclingpath, crs = 3414)
preschool <- st_transform(preschool, crs = 3414)

st_bbox(mpsz14)

     xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
 2667.538 15748.721 56396.440 50256.334 


The bounding box now reports five figure numbers rather than degrees, which confirms the transform did what I wanted.






Warningst_set_crs() against st_transform()



These two look similar and do completely different things, and the chapter uses both, so I want to be able to state the difference precisely.
st_set_crs() changes the label attached to the coordinates without touching a single number. It is an assertion that the numbers were always in the system I am naming. The only correct use for it is when a file arrived with a missing or wrong CRS tag and I know what the right one is. Chapter 1 hits exactly this case, where the shapefile declares SVY21 in its name but carries EPSG 9001 instead of 3414, and st_set_crs(mpsz, 3414) repairs the label without moving anything.
st_transform() recalculates every coordinate into a different system. It is what I need whenever the data really has to move from one system to another.
Using the wrong one produces no error and no warning at any point. Setting a CRS when I should have transformed leaves the numbers in degrees while claiming they are metres, and every downstream area, distance and buffer is silently wrong. This is the most dangerous operation in the chapter, precisely because it fails quietly.




Trying the KML version
The chapter reads one of its layers from KML, and the portal no longer offers that format, so I wrote one out and read it straight back to see what the format costs.

dir.create("data/geospatial/kml", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

st_write(mpsz14,
         "data/geospatial/kml/MP14_Subzone.kml",
         driver = "KML",
         delete_dsn = TRUE,
         quiet = TRUE)

mpsz14_kml <- st_read("data/geospatial/kml/MP14_Subzone.kml", quiet = TRUE)


tibble(
  aspect = c("Attribute columns", "First few column names",
             "Coordinate reference system", "Feature count"),
  geojson = c(as.character(ncol(mpsz14) - 1),
              paste(head(setdiff(names(mpsz14), "geometry"), 4), collapse = ", "),
              st_crs(mpsz14)$input,
              as.character(nrow(mpsz14))),
  kml = c(as.character(ncol(mpsz14_kml) - 1),
          paste(head(setdiff(names(mpsz14_kml), "geometry"), 4), collapse = ", "),
          st_crs(mpsz14_kml)$input,
          as.character(nrow(mpsz14_kml)))
) %>%
  kable(caption = "What survives a round trip through KML")


What survives a round trip through KML







aspect
geojson
kml




Attribute columns
13
2


First few column names
OBJECTID_1, SUBZONE_NO, SUBZONE_N, SUBZONE_C
Name, Description


Coordinate reference system
EPSG:3414
WGS 84


Feature count
323
323











ImportantWhat the round trip destroyed



Two things came back different.
The attribute table collapsed. Every named column, SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, REGION_N and the rest, was flattened into a generic Name field and a Description field containing an HTML fragment. The geometry survived intact but the schema did not, and recovering the attributes would mean parsing them back out of HTML strings.
The coordinate reference system reverted. The KML specification requires WGS84, so st_write() silently reprojected out of the SVY21 metres I had just transformed into. Reading the file back gives me degrees again. If I had carried on working from that object, every area and buffer in the rest of this document would have been wrong, and nothing would have told me.
None of this makes KML a bad format. It is a presentation format designed for drawing things in Google Earth, where a person clicks a shape and reads a description bubble, and for that job an HTML blob is exactly right. GeoJSON and shapefile are analysis formats that keep typed columns and let me declare a projected CRS. The chapter’s instruction predates the portal switching to GeoJSON, and for this work GeoJSON is the best of the three.




Importing and converting aspatial data
The Airbnb listing file has no geometry. It has a latitude column and a longitude column, which is a different thing, and R reads it as an ordinary table.

listings <- read_csv("data/aspatial/listings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

The longitude and latitude columns are gone and a geometry column has appeared in their place, which is what st_as_sf() is for.






WarningTwo arguments that are easy to get backwards



coords takes the x column first and then the y column, so it is longitude before latitude. Writing them the other way round throws no error at all. It places every Singapore listing at roughly 1 degree east and 103 degrees north, which is in the Arctic Ocean somewhere north of Norway, and the only symptom is a map that looks empty because the points are thousands of kilometres outside the frame.
The crs = 4326 here is doing the labelling job, not the transforming job. The numbers in those two columns are already degrees, so I tag them correctly first and only then pipe into st_transform() to get metres. Passing crs = 3414 at this point would claim the degree values were already metres and would put every listing within about a kilometre of the projection origin.



st_bbox(listings_sf)

     xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
 5881.388 22827.701 44899.773 48821.856 


The bounding box falls inside Singapore, so the column order was right.
Following the chapter’s exercise, here is the listings layer drawn over the subzones.

plot(st_geometry(mpsz14))
plot(st_geometry(listings_sf), add = TRUE, col = "red", pch = 20, cex = 0.3)










Geoprocessing, land within five metres of a cycling path
The scenario is that the authority wants to widen the existing cycling network and needs five metres of reserved land on each side. The question is how much land that comes to.

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)
buffer_cycling$AREA <- st_area(buffer_cycling)
sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

4989654 [m^2]



total_ha <- sum(buffer_cycling$AREA) %>% set_units("hectares")
total_ha

498.9654 [hectares]


The dist = 5 means five metres only because the layer is in EPSG:3414. This is the payoff from the transform earlier, and it is invisible in the code. nQuadSegs = 30 controls how many straight segments approximate each quarter circle at the ends and corners of the buffer, so a higher number gives a smoother buffer at the cost of a larger object.






ImportantThe naive sum double counts



st_area() returns a units object, so the sum arrives labelled in square metres and set_units() converts it safely rather than by multiplying by a conversion factor I looked up somewhere.
The bigger issue is that summing the per feature areas counts overlapping land twice. Wherever two cycling paths run close together their five metre buffers intersect, and that shared strip appears in both features. For a land acquisition estimate this overstates the requirement. Dissolving the buffers first fixes it.



dissolved_ha <- buffer_cycling %>%
  st_union() %>%
  st_area() %>%
  set_units("hectares")

dissolved_ha

431.5118 [hectares]



overlap_pct <- as.numeric((total_ha - dissolved_ha) / total_ha * 100)
sprintf("The naive sum overstates the footprint by %.1f percent", overlap_pct)

[1] "The naive sum overstates the footprint by 13.5 percent"


The gap between the two figures is the overlapping land. It is not a rounding difference, and reporting the first number as a land requirement would be a real error in a real project.
The chapter also asks for a plot of the buffers clipped to one subzone, so here is Tampines West.

mpsz_selected <- mpsz14 %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")

buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected)

plot(st_geometry(mpsz_selected))
plot(st_geometry(buffer_cycling_selected), add = TRUE, col = "grey40", border = NA)










Geoprocessing, pre-schools by subzone

mpsz14$PreSch_Count <- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz14, preschool))
summary(mpsz14$PreSch_Count)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   0.00    0.00    4.00    7.09   10.00   72.00 



mpsz14 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, PreSch_Count) %>%
  arrange(desc(PreSch_Count)) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  kable(caption = "Subzones with the most pre-schools")

TipWhat st_intersects() actually returns



It does not return counts. It returns a list with one element for every subzone, and each element holds the row indices of the pre-schools that fall inside that subzone. lengths(), with the s, then measures each element of that list. Using length() without the s would return a single number, the count of subzones, which is not what anyone wants.
Getting indices back rather than a count is more useful than it first looks, because it means I can move from how many to which ones without recomputing anything.
This is also the operation that answers the question of how a computer knows a point sits inside a polygon. It is not running every subzone against every pre-school. It builds a spatial index first, uses bounding boxes to throw out the pairs that cannot possibly intersect, and only runs the exact geometric test on the survivors.


The chapter warns not to confuse st_intersects() with st_intersection(). The first is a predicate that answers whether two geometries touch and hands back indices. The second is a constructor that returns new geometry, the actual overlapping shape, which is what I used above to clip the buffers to Tampines West.


Pre-school density

mpsz14$Area_sqkm <- st_area(mpsz14) %>%
  set_units("km^2") %>%
  as.numeric()

mpsz14$PreSch_Density <- mpsz14$PreSch_Count / mpsz14$Area_sqkm

  select(SUBZONE_N, PreSch_Count, Area_sqkm, PreSch_Density) %>%

The two rankings disagree noticeably. The highest counts sit in large mature residential towns, while the highest densities tend to be small tight subzones where a handful of pre-schools sits on very little land. Which measure is the right one depends entirely on the question. Count answers how much provision exists, density answers how concentrated it is, and neither answers whether the provision is adequate, which would need a denominator of children rather than of land.


Exploratory data analysis

hist(mpsz14$PreSch_Density)








Base hist() is one line and the output is unusable outside my own screen. There is no informative title, the axis labels are the variable expressions, and there is very little room to change any of it.

ggplot(data = mpsz14, aes(x = PreSch_Density)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, colour = "black", fill = "#9C4A2F", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(title = "Pre-school density is heavily right skewed",
       subtitle = "Most subzones sit near zero while a small number reach thirty or more per square kilometre",
       x = "Pre-schools per square kilometre",
       y = "Number of subzones") +
  theme_minimal()








This shape matters a great deal in Part 2. A variable with a long right tail gets carved up very differently by a scheme that divides the value range than by one that divides the count of observations, and the classification section is essentially a test of that.

ggplot(data = mpsz14, aes(x = PreSch_Density, y = PreSch_Count)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#6E7F63", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Count and density are only loosely related",
       subtitle = "A large subzone can hold many pre-schools while still being sparsely provided",
       x = "Pre-schools per square kilometre",
       y = "Pre-school count") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Hands-on Exercise 01: Geospatial Data Wrangling and Choropleth Mapping
text:
Part 2, choropleth mapping
A choropleth shades enumeration units by a value. The useful way to think about it, and the one that makes the classification section make sense, is that it is a histogram with the location put back in. Choosing class breaks is the same act as choosing histogram bins, and nobody would accept arbitrary bins on a histogram without asking what they were.

Importing the data

mpsz19 <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

Reading layer `URA_MP19_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL' from data source 
  `D:\mengtingyu88\geospatial-coursework\Hands-on_Ex\Hands-on_Ex01\data\geospatial\MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson' 
  using driver `GeoJSON'
Simple feature collection with 332 features and 13 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84



names(mpsz19)

 [1] "OBJECTID"   "SUBZONE_NO" "SUBZONE_N"  "SUBZONE_C"  "CA_IND"    
 [6] "PLN_AREA_N" "PLN_AREA_C" "REGION_N"   "REGION_C"   "INC_CRC"   
[11] "FMEL_UPD_D" "SHAPE.AREA" "SHAPE.LEN"  "geometry"  








NoteIf the attribute columns are missing



The GeoJSON I downloaded carries proper named columns. If a version arrives with only Name and Description, the attributes are buried in an HTML table inside Description and have to be parsed out with rvest, which is what the chapter does for its KML file. The code for that case looks like this.

pacman::p_load(rvest)

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

mpsz19 <- mpsz19 %>%
  mutate(
    REGION_N   = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N  = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C  = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())

This is the same schema collapse I measured in the KML round trip earlier, arriving from the other direction.



popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(popdata)

Rows: 100,928
Columns: 7
$ PA   <chr> "Ang Mo Kio", "Ang Mo Kio", "Ang Mo Kio", "Ang Mo Kio", "Ang Mo K…
$ SZ   <chr> "Ang Mo Kio Town Centre", "Ang Mo Kio Town Centre", "Ang Mo Kio T…
$ AG   <chr> "0_to_4", "0_to_4", "0_to_4", "0_to_4", "0_to_4", "0_to_4", "0_to…
$ Sex  <chr> "Males", "Males", "Males", "Males", "Males", "Males", "Males", "M…
$ TOD  <chr> "HDB 1- and 2-Room Flats", "HDB 3-Room Flats", "HDB 4-Room Flats"…
$ Pop  <dbl> 0, 0, 10, 20, 0, 40, 0, 0, 0, 0, 10, 20, 0, 30, 0, 0, 0, 10, 10, …
$ Time <dbl> 2024, 2024, 2024, 2024, 2024, 2024, 2024, 2024, 2024, 2024, 2024,…


The table is in long format. Each row is one combination of planning area, subzone, age group, sex and dwelling type, with a population count attached, so the first job is to collapse everything except the age group away.


Preparing the population table
The chapter defines three age bands and a ratio built from them. Young runs from the 0 to 4 band up to and including 20 to 24. Economically active runs from 25 to 29 up to 60 to 64. Aged is everything from 65 upwards. The dependency ratio is the young plus the aged, divided by the economically active.

popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(POP = sum(Pop), .groups = "drop")

sort(unique(popdata2024$AG))

 [1] "0_to_4"      "10_to_14"    "15_to_19"    "20_to_24"    "25_to_29"   
 [6] "30_to_34"    "35_to_39"    "40_to_44"    "45_to_49"    "5_to_9"     
[11] "50_to_54"    "55_to_59"    "60_to_64"    "65_to_69"    "70_to_74"   
[16] "75_to_79"    "80_to_84"    "85_to_89"    "90_and_over"



popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate(
    age_lower = as.numeric(str_extract(AG, "^\\d+")),
    band = case_when(
      age_lower <= 24 ~ "YOUNG",
      age_lower <= 64 ~ "ACTIVE",
      TRUE            ~ "AGED"
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, band) %>%
  summarise(POP = sum(POP), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = band, values_from = POP, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(
    TOTAL      = YOUNG + ACTIVE + AGED,
    DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / ACTIVE
  )

head(popdata2024) %>% kable(caption = "Population bands by subzone")

ImportantWhy I did not select the age bands by column position



The chapter’s version of this step picks age bands by position, with expressions like rowSums(.[3:6]) and rowSums(.[13:15]). That works on the exact file the chapter was written against and breaks silently on anything else, because pivot_wider() orders the new columns by the order the values first appear in the data rather than alphabetically or numerically. A different sort order in the source file, or one extra age band, moves every index, and the code still runs, just adding up the wrong columns.
Pulling the lower bound out of the band name with a regular expression and then classifying on the number is more code, but it cannot drift. The band boundaries appear once, as 24 and 64, in a place where I can read them and check them against the definition. Printing the unique band names first is what told me 90_and_over parses to 90 rather than to NA, which is the one case where the pattern could have failed.




Joining the population data to the boundaries
The population table keys on subzone name, and the boundary file carries the same names in SUBZONE_N. The thing to watch is case, since the two sources do not agree on it.

mpsz19 <- mpsz19 %>%
  mutate(SUBZONE_N = toupper(SUBZONE_N))

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate(SZ = toupper(str_trim(SZ)),
         PA = toupper(str_trim(PA)))

mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz19, popdata2024,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))

left_join() is used with the spatial object on the left so that the result is still an sf object. Joining the other way round returns a plain tibble with a geometry column that is no longer recognised as geometry, and every subsequent tm_shape() call fails.

tibble(
  metric = c("Subzone polygons",
             "Polygons with no population record",
             "Polygons with zero working age population"),
  n = c(nrow(mpsz_pop2024),
        sum(is.na(mpsz_pop2024$TOTAL)),
        sum(mpsz_pop2024$ACTIVE == 0, na.rm = TRUE))
) %>%
  kable(caption = "Join diagnostics")


Join diagnostics


metric
n




Subzone polygons

Polygons with no population record

Polygons with zero working age population

WarningChecking a join before mapping it



I ran this table before drawing anything, which in hindsight is the single most useful habit in this exercise. A choropleth over a partially failed join looks completely normal. The unmatched areas come out grey and read as missing data rather than as a broken key.
The zero working age rows matter more than they look. Dependency puts ACTIVE in the denominator, so a subzone with residents but nobody aged 25 to 64 produces Inf rather than a large number. Industrial estates, reservoirs, military areas and port land genuinely have no resident working population, so this is real rather than a data error. Mapping Inf shows as an unclassified hole, whereas quietly replacing it with a large number would be inventing data and would also wreck every range based classification scheme further down.



mpsz_pop2024 <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  mutate(DEPENDENCY = ifelse(is.finite(DEPENDENCY), DEPENDENCY, NA_real_))

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.0000  0.6750  0.7283  0.7563  0.8140 10.0000      94 




The quick map with qtm()

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2024, fill = "DEPENDENCY")








tmap_mode("plot") produces a static image and "view" produces an interactive Leaflet map. qtm() is fine for looking at my own data while I work. It is not fine for showing anyone else, because there is no title, no source, no scale and no indication of which classification the default happened to pick.


Building the map from tmap elements
The building block is tm_shape(), which sets the data, followed by one or more layer functions that draw from it. tm_polygons(), tm_symbols(), tm_lines(), tm_raster() and tm_text() are the main ones.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons()








With no arguments the polygons come out light grey with darker grey borders, which confirms the geometry is there before I put a variable on it.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")








tm_polygons() is a wrapper around tm_fill() and tm_borders(), and separating them shows what each contributes.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60", lwd = 0.4, lty = "dashed")








tm_borders() takes col for the border colour, lwd for the line width and lty for the line type, plus fill_alpha for transparency between 0 and 1.
Here is the full version with every element the chapter introduces.

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency\nratio"),
              col = "grey65", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_title("Age dependency ratio by planning subzone, Singapore 2024") +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2, position = c("right", "top")) +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, col = "grey85") +
  tm_credits("Source: Department of Statistics Singapore, and URA Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary",
             position = c("left", "bottom"), size = 0.55) +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE, legend.outside = TRUE)








Each element earns its place for a different reason. tm_grid() gives coordinate context, tm_compass() and tm_scalebar() are the standard cartographic furniture a reader expects, and tm_credits() writes the source onto the image itself so that the attribution survives if someone pulls the figure out of this page and drops it into a slide.


Classification methods
tmap supports ten classification styles, of which fixed, equal, pretty, quantile, jenks, sd, kmeans, hclust, bclust and fisher are the named ones. These are not styling choices. Each one makes a different claim about what the reader ought to be noticing.

make_map <- function(style, title) {
  tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = style, n = 5,
                                                values = "brewer.blues"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE),
                col = "grey70", lwd = 0.2) +
    tm_title(title, size = 0.85)
}

tmap_arrange(
  make_map("equal",    "equal, equal value ranges"),
  make_map("quantile", "quantile, equal counts"),
  make_map("jenks",    "jenks, natural breaks"),
  make_map("sd",       "sd, deviation from the mean"),
  ncol = 2
)














ImportantWhat the four schemes are each saying



Equal interval cuts the value range into bins of equal width. On a skewed variable this pushes almost everything into the bottom class and the map comes out looking empty.
Quantile puts an equal number of subzones into each class. It always produces a visually balanced map, which is both its strength and its trap, because it looks equally convincing when there is no real variation to show.
Jenks minimises variance within classes and so places breaks at genuine gaps in the distribution. It is usually the most faithful to the data, but because the breaks are derived from the data, two Jenks maps of different datasets cannot be compared with each other.
Standard deviation shows distance from the mean, which is a different question. It answers which areas are unusual rather than how much of the thing there is.


Rather than assert that the choice matters, I wanted to see where the subzones actually land.

vals <- mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY[is.finite(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)]

class_counts <- map_dfr(c("equal", "quantile", "jenks", "sd"), function(st) {
  brks <- classIntervals(vals, n = 5, style = st)$brks
  tab  <- table(cut(vals, unique(brks), include.lowest = TRUE))
  tibble(style     = st,
         `class 1` = as.integer(tab[1]), `class 2` = as.integer(tab[2]),
         `class 3` = as.integer(tab[3]), `class 4` = as.integer(tab[4]),
         `class 5` = as.integer(tab[5]))
})

kable(class_counts, caption = "How many subzones land in each class")

WarningOne value can break a whole scheme



The maximum sits far above the median, and it is not a data error. It is a subzone with very few residents whose age mix happens to be lopsided, and a small denominator turns that into a very large ratio.
Equal interval and standard deviation both derive their breaks from the range, so that one subzone stretches the entire scale and everything else falls into the first class. Quantile and Jenks derive their breaks from the ordering and the shape of the distribution instead, so neither of them notices.
The rule I am taking away is that range based classification fails on a variable with outliers. Either use a rank based or distribution based scheme, or handle the outlier explicitly and say in the caption which one was done.


Then the chapter’s exercise on the number of classes.

make_map_n <- function(n) {
  tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = n,
                                                values = "brewer.blues"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE),
                col = "grey70", lwd = 0.2) +
    tm_title(paste0("n = ", n), size = 0.85)
}

tmap_arrange(make_map_n(2), make_map_n(6), make_map_n(10), make_map_n(20),
             ncol = 2)








At two classes the map is a yes or no statement and most of the variation is thrown away. At twenty the classes are narrower than the reader can distinguish by colour, so the extra classes carry information that does not survive being looked at. Somewhere in between is a number that balances the two, and the first section of Part 3 is an attempt to find it rather than guess it.

Custom breaks
For all the built in styles the breakpoints are computed internally. Setting them by hand needs the descriptive statistics first.

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.0000  0.6750  0.7283  0.7563  0.8140 10.0000      94 



tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00),
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency\nratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








The breaks vector includes both a minimum and a maximum, so to end up with five classes I need six values, and they have to be in increasing order. Anything above the top break falls outside the scale and is drawn as missing, which is a real risk on a variable with a long tail.



Colour scheme

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency\nratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5,
                                              values = "-brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency\nratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








The minus prefix reverses the ramp.






NoteSequential against diverging



A sequential palette says the variable runs from less to more with no meaningful midpoint. A diverging palette says there is a midpoint that means something, and that being on one side of it differs in kind rather than in degree.
For a dependency ratio a diverging scheme can be defended if the midpoint is chosen for a reason, such as the national ratio, because a subzone above the national average and one below it really are in different situations. It cannot be defended if the midpoint is just the middle of the observed range, because that invents a threshold that nothing in the data supports.
The reversed map above shows the other half of the problem. Dark now reads as low dependency, which is the opposite of what almost every reader will assume before reading the legend. The code is correct and the communication is not.




Cartographic furniture and layout

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg and SingStat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))









tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5,
                                              values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")









tmap_style("white")

tmap_style() changes the whole layout preset at once, and it is a global setting, so I reset it immediately afterwards. Forgetting to reset it silently restyles every map further down the document, which took me a while to work out the first time it happened.


Small multiple maps
Small multiples put several maps side by side so that a relationship can be read across them. tmap offers three routes to the same idea.

By assigning several variables

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










By arranging separate maps

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"),
                                      item.height = 0.8)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of young population")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"),
                                      item.height = 0.8)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of aged population")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp = 1, ncol = 2)








The difference between these two routes is that assigning several variables forces a shared scale, while tmap_arrange() gives each map its own. A shared scale makes the panels comparable, and separate scales make each panel readable on its own terms. Neither is right in general, and the choice has to follow the question.


By faceting on a grouping variable

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                          values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N", nrow = 2, ncols = 3,
            free.coords = TRUE, drop.units = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








free.coords = TRUE lets each facet zoom to its own region, which makes the small central region readable but destroys any sense of relative size between the panels.



Mapping a selected region

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency\nratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










Adding a statistical chart
A map is good at spatial relationships and poor at distributions, and a chart is the reverse, so putting one inside the other lets a reader check the shape of the data against its geography without leaving the figure.

mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                              values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency\nratio"),
              fill.chart = tm_chart_box()) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(asp = 0.8)








The next step is to find the outliers the box plot is showing and label them on the map itself, so that the reader can see which subzone each dot belongs to.

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)

TipWhy the zoom limits are there



Without set_zoom_limits the reader can zoom out until Singapore is a dot in the South China Sea, or in until a single subzone fills the screen with no context around it. Neither view helps, and both are one scroll away.
Constraining the zoom is a small thing, but it is the same kind of decision as picking class breaks. The map author decides what range of views the argument is being made at, and leaving it open is still a decision, just an unexamined one.
The other habit worth keeping is switching the mode back to "plot" immediately afterwards. tmap_mode() is global, so every map further down the document would otherwise render as an interactive widget, which makes the page heavy and breaks tmap_arrange().

title: Hands-on Exercise 01: Geospatial Data Wrangling and Choropleth Mapping
text:
Part 3, going further
The chapters make three claims in passing that I wanted to test rather than accept. Each of the sections below picks one and puts a number on it.

How many classes is enough
The chapter asks me to compare maps at two, six, ten and twenty classes and note what I see. Looking at them tells me the extremes are bad but not where the useful range sits, so I wanted a measure.
The natural one is the goodness of variance fit, which is the quantity Jenks optimises. It compares the squared deviations of the values from their own class means against the squared deviations from the overall mean. A value near one means the classes capture almost all of the variation in the data, and a value near zero means they capture almost none of it.

gvf <- function(x, style, n) {
  brks <- classIntervals(x, n = n, style = style)$brks
  cls  <- cut(x, unique(brks), include.lowest = TRUE)
  sdam <- sum((x - mean(x))^2)
  sdcm <- sum(tapply(x, cls, function(g) sum((g - mean(g))^2)), na.rm = TRUE)
  1 - sdcm / sdam
}

gvf_grid <- expand_grid(style = c("equal", "quantile", "jenks"),
                        n = 2:10) %>%
  mutate(gvf = map2_dbl(style, n, ~gvf(vals, .x, .y)))

gvf_grid %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = style, values_from = gvf) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3))) %>%
  kable(caption = "Goodness of variance fit by scheme and number of classes")

ImportantWhat this changes about the choice



Two things stand out.
Jenks reaches a high fit at a small number of classes and then flattens off, which is what it is designed to do. Past the point where the curve levels out, each additional class is subdividing variation the reader was already seeing, at the cost of a colour ramp with more steps than anyone can tell apart.
Equal interval sits well below the other two at every number of classes I tested. That is the outlier problem from Part 2 showing up as a number rather than as a map that looks empty. Adding classes barely helps, because the extra breaks all get spent subdividing a part of the range where no subzones live.
So my answer to how many classes is that it depends on the scheme, and that for this variable the honest range is a small number of Jenks classes rather than the arbitrary five I started with. The reason I trust this more than looking at the four maps is that looking at maps mostly measures how good I am at telling shades of blue apart, which is not a property of the data.




Is a subzone boundary a catchment
Counting pre-schools inside a subzone treats the boundary as if it were a wall. In reality a pre-school fifty metres on the other side of the line serves the same children. I wanted to know how much difference that makes, so I recounted using a buffer around each subzone instead of the subzone itself.

mpsz14$PreSch_500m <- lengths(st_intersects(sz_buffer_500, preschool))

  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") %>%

WarningWhat the gap means and what it does not



Every point sits above the equality line, which has to be true since the buffer contains the subzone. The interesting number is how many subzones move from zero to non zero, because those are exactly the ones a reader of the first map would have taken to be unserved.
The buffered count is not a better measure though, only a differently wrong one. It double counts, since a pre-school near a corner falls inside the buffers of several neighbouring subzones at once, so summing the buffered counts across Singapore would give a total far above the number of pre-schools that actually exist. Five hundred metres is also a number I chose rather than derived, and the real catchment of a pre-school depends on how families travel to it.
What this does establish is that a point in polygon count describes the boundary as much as it describes the provision, and that any statement of the form this subzone has no pre-school needs the words within its boundary attached to it. The proper version of this question is a distance based accessibility measure, which comes later in the course.




Does the answer change when the boundaries change
Part 1 uses the 2014 boundary definition and Part 2 uses the 2019 one, because that is what the two chapters specify. That leaves me with two versions of the same geography five years apart, and a chance to check how stable a subzone level result is when the units get redrawn.

ImportantTwo units are not one unit measured twice



The pre-school locations are identical in both calculations. Every difference in the table above comes from the boundaries being drawn in a different place, which is the modifiable areal unit problem in its clearest form.
The correlations are high, which is reassuring for any statement about the broad pattern. The per subzone differences are not zero though, and a claim about one named subzone is only as stable as the boundary that defines it.
There is a second and quieter problem here, which is that the two vintages do not even agree on which subzones exist. Some names appear in one file and not the other, so those rows dropped out of the comparison entirely rather than showing up as a difference. That is worse than a difference, because it is invisible in any table that only compares the matched rows.
The practical consequence for this document is that Part 1 and Part 2 are measured on slightly different geographies, and nothing in the exercise itself flags that. I would not put a Part 1 figure and a Part 2 figure in the same sentence without saying so.

title: Hands-on Exercise 01: Geospatial Data Wrangling and Choropleth Mapping
text:
Limitations
The pre-school counts and the population figures come from different boundary vintages, 2014 and 2019, since that is what the two chapters specify. The section above measures how much that matters rather than fixing it.
The dependency ratio follows the chapter’s definition, where young runs to 24 and active starts at 25. The more common international convention puts the split at 15. With high tertiary participation in Singapore the chapter’s version is arguably the better description, but it is a convention either way, and the ratio here is not comparable to figures computed the other way.
Subzones with residents but no working age residents were set to NA and drop out of every map. There are not many, and they are dropped rather than shown as zero, which is a choice that leaves small holes in the map.
The buffer analysis in Part 3 uses a 500 metre radius that I picked because it is a plausible walking distance, not because anything in the data supports it. A different radius would give different numbers, and I have not tested how sensitive the conclusion is to that choice.
Nothing in this exercise tests whether the spatial patterns are real. Every map here could look much the same if the values had been assigned to subzones at random, and I have no way yet to tell the difference. That is what the spatial weights and autocorrelation topics later in the course are for.

title: Hands-on Exercise 01: Geospatial Data Wrangling and Choropleth Mapping
text:
Reflection
Most of the mechanics here were familiar. Reading files, joining tables and drawing charts are the same operations I already know, under different function names. Three things were genuinely new.
The first is that the coordinate reference system is a correctness problem rather than a formatting one. The distinction between st_set_crs() and st_transform() has no real equivalent in ordinary data work, and getting it wrong produces no error, no warning, and a perfectly plausible looking number that happens to be wrong by five orders of magnitude.
The second is that classification is a decision I make whether or not I think about it. Accepting the qtm() default is still choosing something. Computing the goodness of variance fit was the most useful thing I did in Part 3, because it turned a vague instruction to compare the maps into a number I could act on.
The third is how much of the work turned out to be checking rather than analysing. The join diagnostics, the Inf handling, the buffer overlap correction and the boundary vintage comparison are none of them in the chapters, and each one was a place where I could have produced a wrong answer that looked completely reasonable. If I did this again I would run the join diagnostic before drawing the first map rather than after it, because I had already made a choropleth over data I had not verified, and it looked fine.

text:
A note on reproducibility
Each page shows the code that produced every figure and table. Where a dataset is small enough, it is stored alongside the analysis in this repository. Where it is not, the source and the download steps are documented at the top of the page so that the work can be repeated from scratch.
I use Quarto’s freeze feature, which caches computed results and only re-executes a page when its source changes. This keeps the site fast to rebuild, but it also means the committed output reflects the last successful run rather than a fresh run on every deploy.

title: About
text:
Projections
All analysis in this portfolio uses SVY21 (EPSG:3414) as the projected coordinate reference system. Singapore geospatial data arrives in a mixture of SVY21 and WGS84 (EPSG:4326), and any calculation involving distance, area, or spatial weights requires a projected CRS rather than a geographic one. Where a dataset needs converting, the transformation step is shown explicitly rather than assumed.

title: Hands-on Exercise 02: Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
The first exercise was about getting data into a usable state and drawing it. This one is about asking whether what the drawing shows is real.
Two questions run through the whole thing. Are childcare centres in Singapore randomly distributed, and if they are not, where are the concentrations. The first question sounds trivial and is not, because answering it properly means saying what random would have looked like, and that turns out to be the hardest decision in the exercise.
Part 1 assembles the analytical sandbox and converts the data into the object classes that spatstat needs. Part 2 covers first order analysis, which is about intensity, so nearest neighbour testing and kernel density estimation. Part 3 repeats the analysis at planning area level for four towns. Part 4 covers second order analysis with the G, F, K and L functions, which are about the relationships between points rather than their density.
Part 5 is my own. Three of the choices the chapters make quietly turn out to change the answer, and I wanted to measure by how much rather than take them on trust.






NoteReference



Chapter 4, First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods, and Chapter 5, 2nd Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods, from the course reference guide.

title: Hands-on Exercise 02: Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
Getting started

pacman::p_load(sf, spatstat, terra, tmap, tidyverse, knitr)


set.seed(1234)

The seed goes near the top rather than buried next to the first simulation. Every Monte Carlo result below depends on it, and having it in one visible place is the difference between a document that reruns identically and one that does not.
spatstat is worth a word because it is not one package. Installing it pulls in spatstat.geom for the object classes and geometry, spatstat.explore for the exploratory tools including the Clark-Evans test and the G, F, K and L functions, spatstat.model for fitting, and several more. Loading spatstat loads the family. This matters when reading the documentation, since the help pages live under the sub-package names.
terra appears only at the end of the first order section, where it converts a spatstat pixel image into a raster that tmap can draw properly.






NoteWhat I did not need



The chapter loads rvest to pull attribute fields out of an HTML fragment. That step is needed when the subzone boundary comes in as KML, where the attribute table has been flattened into a description bubble. I am reusing the GeoJSON I downloaded for the first exercise, which keeps SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N and REGION_N as proper typed columns, so there is nothing to parse and rvest never comes into it.
This is the same difference between presentation formats and analysis formats that I measured in the first exercise when I wrote a layer out to KML and read it back. It is nice to see the cost show up again as work I did not have to do.

TipWhy st_zm() is here



Singapore geospatial files often carry a Z dimension holding an elevation that is zero for every feature, left over from the KML lineage of the data. It is harmless in sf, where it simply shows up as XYZ in the geometry type.
It is not harmless in spatstat. A planar point pattern is planar, and as.ppp() on a three dimensional geometry either errors or silently drops the third value depending on the version. Dropping it explicitly here means the conversion later has nothing to complain about.
The what = "ZM" argument removes both Z and M, where M is a measure dimension used for things like distance along a route. Neither carries information in this data.




Removing the offshore islands

mpsz_cl <- mpsz_sf %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N != "SOUTHERN GROUP",
         PLN_AREA_N != "WESTERN ISLANDS",
         PLN_AREA_N != "NORTH-EASTERN ISLANDS")

tibble(
  stage = c("All subzones", "After removing offshore islands", "Removed"),
  n = c(nrow(mpsz_sf), nrow(mpsz_cl), nrow(mpsz_sf) - nrow(mpsz_cl))
) %>%
  kable(caption = "Subzones kept for the analysis window")


Subzones kept for the analysis window


stage
n




All subzones
332


After removing offshore islands
327


Removed
5











ImportantWhy the islands have to go, and what it costs



The chapter drops these three groups without saying why, and the reason turns out to be central to everything that follows.
Every test in this document compares the observed pattern against a null in which points are scattered uniformly at random over an observation window. That window is the study area. Leaving Pulau Ubin, the Southern Islands and the Western Islands in the window means the null model expects childcare centres to be spread across water and across islands with almost no residents. Against a null that unrealistic, any real settlement pattern comes out clustered, and the test stops being informative.
The cost is that I have now made a decision that shapes the answer. A smaller and more realistic window makes the null harder to reject, which is the honest direction to err in, but the window is still mine rather than the data’s. Part 5 measures how much the choice matters.



plot(st_geometry(mpsz_cl))










Importing the childcare centres

childcare_sf <- st_read("data/geospatial/ChildCareServices.geojson") %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

Reading layer `CHILDCARE' from data source 
  `D:\mengtingyu88\geospatial-coursework\Hands-on_Ex\Hands-on_Ex02\data\geospatial\ChildCareServices.geojson' 
  using driver `GeoJSON'
Simple feature collection with 1925 features and 16 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6878 ymin: 1.247759 xmax: 103.9897 ymax: 1.462134
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84



st_crs(childcare_sf)$input

[1] "EPSG:3414"

st_bbox(childcare_sf)

    xmin     ymin     xmax     ymax 
11810.03 25596.33 45404.24 49300.88 


Both layers now report SVY21 and their bounding boxes are in the same numeric range, which is the check that the two are actually in the same spatial context rather than merely both claiming to be.


Mapping the two layers together

tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(mpsz_cl) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey60", lwd = 0.3) +
tm_shape(childcare_sf) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.04, fill = "#9C4A2F") +
  tm_title("Childcare centres and planning subzones") +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2, position = c("right", "top")) +
  tm_credits("Source: ECDA and URA, via data.gov.sg",
             position = c("left", "bottom"), size = 0.55)








The points fall inside the polygons, which confirms the two layers share a coordinate system. This sounds like a formality and is the check that would have caught a wrong projection before any statistics were computed on top of it.

tmap_mode("view")

tm_shape(childcare_sf) +
  tm_dots()






tmap_mode("plot")

The interactive version is useful for a different reason. Zooming in shows that centres cluster along HDB estate spines and thin out over industrial land and reservoirs, which is the pattern the statistics will later confirm, and seeing it first makes the numbers easier to trust.






WarningInteractive maps are not free



Each interactive map holds an open connection and embeds a full Leaflet widget in the page. More than a handful in one document makes the html heavy and slow to load. I use two in this exercise and switch back to plot mode straight after each.
The bigger risk is forgetting the switch. tmap_mode() is global, so an unclosed view mode turns every later map into a widget, including the small multiples, which then fail to arrange.

title: Hands-on Exercise 02: Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
Part 2, converting to spatstat classes
spatstat does not work with sf. It has its own object classes, ppp for a planar point pattern and owin for the observation window, and getting the data into them cleanly is most of the work in this section.

Creating the ppp object

childcare_ppp <- as.ppp(childcare_sf)
class(childcare_ppp)

                    (33590 x 23700 units)
Window area = 796335000 square units


The summary reports the object as a marked point pattern, because the two attribute columns from the GeoJSON came across as marks. That is not what I want here. Every test below is about where the points are and none of them is about what the points are, and marks make envelope() harder to reason about because the simulated patterns have to decide what to do with them.

childcare_ppp <- unmark(childcare_ppp)
summary(childcare_ppp)

Planar point pattern:  1925 points
Average intensity 2.417323e-06 points per square unit

*Pattern contains duplicated points*

Coordinates are given to 11 decimal places

Window: rectangle = [11810.03, 45404.24] x [25596.33, 49300.88] units
                    (33590 x 23700 units)
Window area = 796335000 square units




Checking for duplicated points

any(duplicated(childcare_ppp))

[1] TRUE

sum(multiplicity(childcare_ppp) > 1)

[1] 338








ImportantCoincident points break the distance functions



This check is not in the chapter and it needs to be, because several childcare centres in Singapore share an address. Two centres in the same HDB block, or on different floors of the same building, geocode to exactly the same coordinate pair.
A pattern with coincident points is not a valid input to the nearest neighbour machinery. The distance from one of a coincident pair to its nearest neighbour is zero, which pushes the G function up at r equal to zero and drags the Clark-Evans R statistic down. Both effects say clustered, and both are artefacts of the geocoding rather than facts about where childcare centres are.
spatstat will warn about this when the K and L functions run. Fixing it first is better than reading past the warning.



childcare_ppp_jit <- rjitter(childcare_ppp,
                             retry = TRUE,
                             nsim = 1,
                             drop = TRUE)

any(duplicated(childcare_ppp_jit))

[1] FALSE


Jittering moves each point by a small random amount, which separates the coincident ones without meaningfully changing the pattern at the scales this analysis looks at. The alternative is to drop duplicates, which would understate provision in exactly the dense areas the analysis is about. Jittering keeps the count honest and I have recorded that I did it.


Creating the owin object

sg_owin <- as.owin(mpsz_cl)
class(sg_owin)

[1] "owin"



plot(sg_owin)










Combining the points and the window

childcareSG_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[sg_owin]
childcareSG_ppp

Planar point pattern: 1925 points
window: polygonal boundary
enclosing rectangle: [2667.54, 55941.94] x [21448.47, 50256.33] units



tibble(
  stage = c("Points in the raw layer",
            "Points inside the study window",
            "Points dropped"),
  n = c(npoints(childcare_ppp),
        npoints(childcareSG_ppp),
        npoints(childcare_ppp) - npoints(childcareSG_ppp))
) %>%
  kable(caption = "What the window clipping removed")


What the window clipping removed


stage
n




Points in the raw layer

Points inside the study window
1925


Points dropped
