title: Take-home Exercise 2
text:
9.4 Reading the EHSA clusters

9.4.1 New hot spots and the corrected cold spots
After the correction no township is an intensifying hot spot for any variable. Mogaung and Hpakant in Kachin are new hot spots for explosions, significantly hot only in the final quarter, 2025 Q3. Hpakant recorded 56 explosion events in that quarter, its highest in the study period, together with 48 and 50 battles in 2025 Q2 and Q3. Mogaung itself recorded a single explosion event in 2025 Q3. It is classed as a new hot spot because Gi* counts its neighbour Hpakant, which shows how the statistic flags a neighbourhood rather than a single township.
The reclassified townships, Khaunglanhpu in Kachin, Nansang, Langkho and Mongpan in southern Shan, Mongyang in eastern Shan and Narphan and Pangwaun in the Wa area, are now diminishing cold spots. Their own counts stayed at zero or one event almost every quarter. For a neighbourhood of zeros, Gi* depends only on how unevenly events are spread across the country. The coefficient of variation of quarterly explosion counts across townships rose from about 1.6 in 2021 and 2022 to about 2.4 in 2025, as events concentrated in fewer townships, and a neighbourhood with no events looks less unusual against that background. The diminishing trend therefore reflects a change in the national distribution. No new violence has reached these townships.


9.4.2 Consecutive hot spots
A consecutive hot spot has an unbroken run of significant hot quarters at the end of the series and was never hot before that run. For battles there are three, Mogoke in Mandalay and Kyaukme and Nawnghkio in northern Shan. All three sit on the road from Mandalay to Lashio, and Kyaukme and Nawnghkio were contested after the second phase of Operation 1027 in mid 2024. Mogoke and Kyaukme are also consecutive hot spots for explosions, together with Hpapun in Kayin and Shwegyin and Kyaukkyi in Bago (East).
For violence against civilians the consecutive hot spots are Taungtha, Kyaukpadaung and Mahlaing in Mandalay and Yenangyaung in Magway. These are southern Dry Zone townships close to the military’s core areas around Meiktila and Nay Pyi Taw, which suggests attacks on civilians spreading south from the Sagaing heartland.


9.4.3 Oscillating hot spots
Oscillating hot spots are hot in the latest quarter but were significantly cold at some earlier point. This is the largest hot category, with 16 townships for battles, 23 for explosions and 9 for violence against civilians, and their mean tau is between 0.53 and 0.66. In practice these are townships that started cold and turned hot.
For battles they form two groups. One is around Mandalay city, covering Pyinoolwin, Madaya, Singu, Thabeikkyin, Kyaukse, Taungtha and Ngazun. The other is in southern Tanintharyi and on Ramree island and the Kyaukpyu coast in Rakhine, where the Arakan Army advanced in 2024. The explosions group adds Dawei, Launglon, Thayetchaung, Bago (East), Pakokku and Nyaung-U. The pattern is fighting moving toward the military’s strongholds around Mandalay and the coast.


9.4.4 Sporadic hot spots
Sporadic hot spots switch on and off and have never been significantly cold. For battles there are 16, and their mean tau is negative at minus 0.38. They include Kale, Kalewa, Mingin, Katha and Kani in Sagaing, Demoso, Hpasawng and Mese in Kayah, Hakha in Chin and Gangaw and Tilin in Magway. These are places of heavy fighting in 2021 and 2022 that have quieted since, because the resistance took control of large rural areas and front lines moved elsewhere. For violence against civilians most of the 20 sporadic hot spots are in Sagaing and Mandalay, including the five townships of Mandalay city.


9.4.5 Oscillating and consecutive cold spots
For battles, the seven oscillating cold spots are Muse, Namhkan, Kutkai, Kunlong and Laukkaing in northern Shan and Kanpetlet and Paletwa in Chin. Their tau averages minus 0.46. These townships were hot during Operation 1027 and are now significantly cold. In northern Shan this follows the ceasefires brokered by China between the military and the MNDAA and TNLA. In Paletwa it follows the Arakan Army’s capture of the township in early 2024.
Consecutive cold spots for explosions and violence against civilians are in Yangon, such as Kyauktada, Thongwa, Seikgyikanaungto, Sanchaung, Dagon and Thanlyin, and in the delta around Pyapon and Bogale. Yangon was a site of urban bombings and arrests in 2021 and 2022 and has become significantly cold in recent quarters.


9.4.6 Sporadic cold spots
This is the largest category, with 35 townships for battles, 56 for explosions and 70 for violence against civilians. They cover Yangon, the delta, Bago and southern Magway, which are areas the military still holds. Each has at least one significantly cold quarter but has never been significantly hot. I read these as places where violence stays low with occasional incidents. They are not guaranteed safe zones.






TipMy takeaway



The LMSA maps told me the Dry Zone is the centre of the war. EHSA showed that the centre is not where change is happening. Most Sagaing townships drop out of the EHSA maps because they have been hot for so long that their Gi* series has no significant trend. The growth is in the ring around Mandalay, the Mandalay to Lashio road, Hpakant in Kachin and the Rakhine and Tanintharyi coasts.

title: Take-home Exercise 2
text:
10.1 The question
The Low-Low clusters for battles cover Yangon, the delta and Bago, and it would be easy to read them as safe. Yet Yangon recorded 1,460 explosion events and 765 attacks on civilians. Univariate LISA and EHSA compare a township only with its neighbours on the same variable, so they cannot show violence that happens where there is little fighting around it.
I use a bivariate Local Moran’s I to compare each township’s level of one type of violence with the level of battles in its neighbourhood. A High-Low result marks a township with heavy violence surrounded by little fighting. That is violence away from the front line, and it calls for a different protection response from violence on the front line.

title: Take-home Exercise 2
text:
10.2 Method
The bivariate statistic for township i is the standardised value of variable x at i multiplied by the spatial lag of the standardised battle count y around i. Significance comes from permuting the neighbours of i. I run it for three x variables.

Military air and drone strikes, the Air/drone strike sub-event with actor Military Forces of Myanmar (2021-). This tests whether strikes follow the front or reach beyond it.
Remote explosives, landmines and IEDs, the bombs used in urban attacks.
Violence against civilians.

The neighbourhood is the same row-standardised queen contiguity used in Section 8, without the township itself, so the comparison is always against the surrounding battle level.


Code
bv_inputs <- acled_ts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(bv_var = case_when(
    sub_event_type == "Air/drone strike" &
      actor1 == "Military Forces of Myanmar (2021-)" ~ "air",
    sub_event_type == "Remote explosive/landmine/IED" ~ "ied",
    var == "vac" ~ "vac",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_)) |>
  filter(!is.na(bv_var)) |>
  count(TS_PCODE, bv_var) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = bv_var, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

mmr_bv <- mmr_conflict |>
  select(ST, TS, TS_PCODE, battles) |>
  left_join(bv_inputs, by = "TS_PCODE") |>
  mutate(across(c(air, ied, vac), ~ replace_na(.x, 0L)))

title: Take-home Exercise 2
text:
10.3 Findings
Military air strikes stay with the fighting. There is not a single significant High-Low township for air and drone strikes. Most of the 40 significant High-High townships sit inside the battle clusters of Sagaing, Magway, Mandalay and Kayin found in the LMSA. The Low-High townships, such as Dawei, Matupi and Hakha, have heavy fighting around them but relatively few recorded strikes. At township scale the military’s air campaign concentrates where it is fighting, and no township stands out as a target of strikes far from the front.
Bombs and attacks on civilians do not. IEDs have 20 significant High-Low townships and 18 of them are in Yangon, including Hlaingtharya (East) with 103 IED events, North Okkalapa with 83 and Insein with 78, each surrounded by townships averaging only a few battles. Bago and Magway towns complete the list. Violence against civilians has 11 High-Low townships, nine in Yangon and two in Magway, Taungdwingyi and Natmauk.
These are the townships the univariate maps called Low-Low or cold. The bivariate result shows them as places where civilians face bombings, targeted killings and arrests without an active front line nearby. Most of this violence is urban guerrilla attacks by resistance cells and reprisals by the military and allied militias such as Pyu Saw Htee.

title: Take-home Exercise 2
text:
10.4 Assumptions and limitations
The analysis assumes battle counts are a fair proxy for where the front line is. A township can be contested without frequent recorded battles, for example under siege. The bivariate statistic measures co-location only, so a High-High result does not prove that strikes were a response to battles. ACLED attributes some drone strikes to the military when the actor is uncertain, and in remote areas air strikes may be under-reported. Finally, the Yangon results are partly a product of its very small townships. A single urban bombing campaign shows up across several neighbouring units, which raises their count compared with large rural townships.

title: Take-home Exercise 2

title: Hands-on Ex09: Hedonic Pricing Models with Geographically Weighted Regression
text:
This exercise builds a hedonic pricing model for condominium resale prices in Singapore. A hedonic model treats the price of a unit as the sum of what buyers pay for each of its features, such as floor area, age, tenure and how close the unit is to the CBD, an MRT station or a park.
The data covers 1,436 resale transactions in 2015. The dependent variable is SELLING_PRICE. The independent variables fall into two groups, structural ones that describe the unit and its development, and locational ones that measure the distance to different facilities.
An ordinary least squares (OLS) model gives one coefficient per variable for the whole island. Geographically weighted regression (GWR) fits a separate weighted regression at every sale and gives nearby sales more weight, so each coefficient can change from place to place. The GWmodel package does the calibration.
The work has six parts. Part 1 and Part 2 prepare the boundary layer and the transaction data. Part 3 explores the data. Part 4 builds the OLS model and tests its assumptions, including spatial autocorrelation in the residuals. Part 5 calibrates GWR with a fixed and an adaptive bandwidth and maps the output. Part 6 adds six checks and alternatives of my own.

title: Hands-on Ex09: Hedonic Pricing Models with Geographically Weighted Regression
text:
Setting up

The data
Two datasets are used.








Dataset
Type
What it holds




MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL
polygon shapefile
URA Master Plan 2014 planning subzone boundaries, 323 subzones in SVY21


Condo_resale_2015.csv
csv
1,436 condominium resale transactions in 2015 with 23 fields



The csv gives the location of each unit in latitude and longitude, the selling price, the floor area, the age, the number of units in the development, three dummy variables for family friendliness and tenure, and 13 proximity fields with the distance from the unit to the CBD, the nearest MRT station, park, primary school, shopping mall and other facilities.
I put the shapefile in data/geospatial and the csv in data/aspatial. The course notes use chap13/data/..., so I changed every path to match this layout. The csv was prepared for the course, so I keep the data folder out of the public repository as I did for Ex07 and Ex08.


Packages
The course page loads eleven packages. olsrr, performance and gtsummary handle the OLS model and its diagnostics, corrplot draws the correlation matrix, ggpubr arranges the histograms, sf and sfdep handle the spatial data and the Moran’s I test, GWmodel calibrates GWR, tmap draws the maps, and tidyverse and RColorBrewer cover the rest. I added see, which supplies the plot methods behind the performance checks.


Show the code
pacman::p_load(olsrr, corrplot, ggpubr,
               sf, sfdep, GWmodel, tmap,
               tidyverse, gtsummary,
               performance, see, RColorBrewer)




A note on GWmodel
GWmodel covers the geographically weighted (GW) family of methods. It includes GW summary statistics, GW principal components analysis, GW discriminant analysis and several forms of GW regression, and some of them come in a robust version that resists outliers. The outputs are usually mapped, and the maps work as an exploratory step that shows where a global model breaks down and which variables deserve a closer look. This exercise uses bw.gwr() to choose the bandwidth and gwr.basic() to fit the model.

  geom_histogram(bins = 20,

The histogram is strongly right skewed. Half of the units sold between 1.1 and 1.95 million, and a thin tail stretches to 18 million.


Show the code

  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarise(above_5m = sum(SELLING_PRICE > 5e6),

1       34 6662500.


Only 34 sales are above 5 million and the 99th percentile is 6.66 million. These few sales stretch the x axis so far that nearly all the bars are pressed against the left edge.
A log transformation pulls the tail in. mutate() adds LOG_SELLING_PRICE to the sf data frame.


Show the code

  mutate(`LOG_SELLING_PRICE` = log(SELLING_PRICE))

       aes(x = `LOG_SELLING_PRICE`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")









The log histogram is much closer to a bell shape, though it still leans to the right. I measured the skewness of both versions to put a number on the change.

                 fill = "light blue")

PROX_ELDERLYCARE <- ggplot(data = condo_resale.sf,
                           aes(x = `PROX_ELDERLYCARE`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA <- ggplot(data = condo_resale.sf,
                               aes(x = `PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

PROX_HAWKER_MARKET <- ggplot(data = condo_resale.sf,
                             aes(x = `PROX_HAWKER_MARKET`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

PROX_KINDERGARTEN <- ggplot(data = condo_resale.sf,
                            aes(x = `PROX_KINDERGARTEN`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

PROX_MRT <- ggplot(data = condo_resale.sf,
                   aes(x = `PROX_MRT`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

PROX_PARK <- ggplot(data = condo_resale.sf,
                    aes(x = `PROX_PARK`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

PROX_PRIMARY_SCH <- ggplot(data = condo_resale.sf,
                           aes(x = `PROX_PRIMARY_SCH`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH <- ggplot(data = condo_resale.sf,
                               aes(x = `PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

ggarrange(AREA_SQM, AGE, PROX_CBD, PROX_CHILDCARE,
          PROX_ELDERLYCARE, PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA,
          PROX_HAWKER_MARKET, PROX_KINDERGARTEN, PROX_MRT,
          PROX_PARK, PROX_PRIMARY_SCH, PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH,
          ncol = 3, nrow = 4)









Most of the proximity variables are right skewed. Eight of the ten distance histograms rise quickly from zero and trail off to the right, which fits facilities that are common across the island, since most units are close to a childcare centre, a park or an MRT station and a few are far away. PROX_CHILDCARE is the most extreme, with almost every unit within 0.5 km and a small group between 2.5 and 3.5 km.
AREA_SQM has the same shape as the price, with half the units between 103 and 156 square metres and a few above 400. The OLS assumptions concern the residuals and say nothing about the shape of the predictors. Even so, these far out values give a handful of sales a strong pull on the fitted line.
AGE, PROX_CBD and PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA are spread more evenly. AGE has a second bump at around 30 years, a group of older developments. PROX_CBD spreads from under 1 km to 19 km with several peaks, which follows the way condominiums cluster in a few parts of the island.


3.3 Statistical point map
The interactive maps on this page draw the subzones from a simplified copy of the boundary layer. The callout below explains why.


Show the code
mpsz_view <- st_simplify(mpsz_svy21,
                         dTolerance = 10,
                         preserveTopology = TRUE)








NoteKeeping the interactive maps light



My first render of this page produced about 77 MB of markdown, and pandoc was still working on it after ten minutes. In view mode tmap stores a popup for every feature with all of its columns, so each GWR map carried 52 values for each of the 1,436 sales and weighed about 19 MB on its own. I limited the popups to a few relevant fields with popup = tm_popup(vars = ...), and I drew the subzones from mpsz_view, simplified with st_simplify() at a 10 m tolerance. That cuts the boundary from 55,793 vertices to 9,657 with no visible change at zoom levels 11 to 14. Every calculation and static map still uses the full mpsz_svy21.


The interactive map below colours each sale by its price in five quantile classes.


Show the code
tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(mpsz_view) +
  tm_polygons(popup = tm_popup(vars = c("SUBZONE_N", "PLN_AREA_N"))) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +
  tm_dots(fill = "SELLING_PRICE",
          fill_alpha = 0.6,
          size = 0.5,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile"),
          popup = tm_popup(vars = c("SELLING_PRICE", "AREA_SQM",
                                    "AGE", "PROX_CBD"))) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(11, 14))







Show the code
tmap_mode("plot")


The course draws the points with tm_dots(), and set_zoom_limits in tm_view() keeps the zoom level between 11 and 14. The last line switches tmap back to plot mode.
The expensive sales cluster in the centre. The top class, 2.13 to 18 million, is packed around Orchard, Newton, River Valley and Tanglin, with smaller groups along the east coast and on Sentosa. The cheapest classes sit mostly in the north around Woodlands, Yishun and Sembawang and in the outer parts of the east and west.
To put numbers on the map, I joined each sale to its planning region and planning area with st_join(). I reuse condo_region in Part 6.


Show the code
condo_region <- st_join(condo_resale.sf,
                        mpsz_svy21 %>%
                          select(REGION_N, PLN_AREA_N))

condo_region %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(REGION_N) %>%
  summarise(sales = n(),
            median_price = median(SELLING_PRICE),
            median_price_psm = median(SELLING_PRICE / AREA_SQM))


# A tibble: 5 × 4
  REGION_N          sales median_price median_price_psm
  <chr>             <int>        <dbl>            <dbl>
1 CENTRAL REGION      653      1940000           14865.
2 EAST REGION         305      1132500            9652.
3 NORTH REGION         81       888888            9248.
4 NORTH-EAST REGION   145      1212544           10696.
5 WEST REGION         252      1250000           10324.


The Central Region accounts for 653 of the 1,436 sales, and its median price of 1.94 million is more than double the North Region’s 0.89 million. The gap holds after allowing for size, since the median price per square metre is 14,865 in the Central Region and between 9,248 and 10,696 in the other four.

title: Hands-on Ex09: Hedonic Pricing Models with Geographically Weighted Regression
section: Part 4 Hedonic pricing model with OLS
text:
Part 4 Hedonic pricing model with OLS

4.1 Simple linear regression
The first model explains SELLING_PRICE with AREA_SQM alone. lm() returns an object of class lm, and summary() prints the coefficients and the fit statistics.


Show the code
condo.slr <- lm(formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM,
                data = condo_resale.sf)
summary(condo.slr)



Call:
lm(formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM, data = condo_resale.sf)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-3695815  -391764   -87517   258900 13503875 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -258121.1    63517.2  -4.064 5.09e-05 ***
AREA_SQM      14719.0      428.1  34.381  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 942700 on 1434 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4518,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4515 
F-statistic:  1182 on 1 and 1434 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The fitted line is
\[
\widehat{SELLING\_PRICE} = -258{,}121.1 + 14{,}719 \times AREA\_SQM
\]
Each extra square metre adds about 14,719 to the price. The negative intercept has no practical meaning, since no unit has zero floor area.
Floor area alone explains 45.2% of the variation in price (R² = 0.4518). The F statistic of 1,182 on 1 and 1,434 degrees of freedom has a p-value below 2.2e-16, so I reject the null hypothesis that the mean price predicts as well as the model. Both the intercept and the slope have p-values below 0.001, so I also reject the null hypothesis that either one is zero.
geom_smooth(method = lm) draws the fitted line on the scatter plot.


Show the code
ggplot(data = condo_resale.sf,
       aes(x = `AREA_SQM`, y = `SELLING_PRICE`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm)









Most points sit close to the line below 200 square metres, and the spread widens as the units get bigger. A few sales lie far above the line. The highest, an 18 million sale of a 323 square metre unit in Tanglin, sits about 13.5 million above it. Several units of 400 to 470 square metres sit well below the line at 2.5 to 3.9 million, so floor area alone cannot separate a large unit in a prime location from one in the suburbs.


4.2 Checking the independent variables for correlation
Before putting all the variables into one model, I check whether any pair is highly correlated. Strongly correlated predictors inflate the variance of the coefficients and make them hard to interpret, which is known as multicollinearity. corrplot() draws the correlation matrix of columns 5 to 23, which are all the variables except the coordinates, the postcode and the price.


Show the code
corrplot(cor(condo_resale[, 5:23]),
         diag = FALSE,
         order = "AOE",
         tl.pos = "td",
         tl.cex = 0.5,
         method = "number",
         type = "upper")









The order = "AOE" option sorts the variables by the angular order of the eigenvectors, a method suggested by Michael Friendly, so that variables with similar correlation patterns sit next to each other. The other options are "FPC", "hclust" and "alphabet".
The matrix has 171 pairs and the printed numbers are hard to read at this size, so I listed the pairs above 0.5 in absolute value.


Show the code
cor_mat <- cor(condo_resale[, 5:23])
cor_mat[lower.tri(cor_mat, diag = TRUE)] <- NA

as.data.frame(as.table(cor_mat)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Freq), abs(Freq) > 0.5) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(Freq)))


                Var1                 Var2       Freq
1           FREEHOLD       LEASEHOLD_99YR -0.8356654
2     PROX_CHILDCARE        PROX_BUS_STOP  0.7708911
3     PROX_CHILDCARE     PROX_PRIMARY_SCH  0.6255029
4           PROX_MRT        PROX_BUS_STOP  0.5560678
5     PROX_CHILDCARE             PROX_MRT  0.5319302
6   PROX_PRIMARY_SCH        PROX_BUS_STOP  0.5251440
7           PROX_CBD   PROX_HAWKER_MARKET  0.5245050
8 PROX_HAWKER_MARKET PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH  0.5201978
9           PROX_MRT     PROX_PRIMARY_SCH  0.5015034


FREEHOLD and LEASEHOLD_99YR have the strongest correlation at -0.84, so only one of them should go into the model. The course keeps FREEHOLD and drops LEASEHOLD_99YR (the course text calls it LEASE_99YEAR). The next pair is PROX_CHILDCARE and PROX_BUS_STOP at 0.77, and every other pair is at 0.63 or below.
Two dummies that split every unit into two tenures would correlate at exactly -1, so I cross tabulated them to see where the gap comes from.


Show the code
table(FREEHOLD = condo_resale$FREEHOLD,
      LEASEHOLD_99YR = condo_resale$LEASEHOLD_99YR)


        LEASEHOLD_99YR
FREEHOLD   0   1
       0 128 701
       1 607   0


607 units are freehold, 701 are on a 99 year lease, and 128 are neither, most likely 999 year or other long leases. With LEASEHOLD_99YR dropped, those 128 units join the 99 year units in the baseline, so the FREEHOLD coefficient compares freehold units against every other tenure.


4.3 Multiple linear regression
lm() calibrates the full model with 18 independent variables, and summary() prints the output.


Show the code
condo.mlr <- lm(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_HAWKER_MARKET +
    PROX_KINDERGARTEN + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH +
    PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS +
    FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf)
summary(condo.mlr)

lm(formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE + PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + 
    PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_HAWKER_MARKET + 
    PROX_KINDERGARTEN + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + 
    PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD, 
    data = condo_resale.sf)

PROX_MRT             -314599.68   57947.44  -5.429 6.66e-08 ***

R² rises from 0.452 to 0.652. Four variables are not significant at the 5% level, PROX_HAWKER_MARKET (p = 0.418), PROX_KINDERGARTEN (p = 0.075), PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH (p = 0.911) and PROX_SUPERMARKET (p = 0.560).


4.4 Revising the model
The revised model drops the four variables.


Show the code
condo.mlr1 <- lm(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_MRT +
    PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA +
    PROX_PARK + PROX_PRIMARY_SCH +
    PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_BUS_STOP +
    NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf)
summary(condo.mlr1)

All 14 remaining variables are significant at the 1% level, and R² barely moves, from 0.6518 to 0.6507. Dropping variables one at a time by their p-values can mislead when they are related, so I also tested the four together with a partial F test.


Show the code
anova(condo.mlr1, condo.mlr)


Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE + PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + 
    PROX_MRT + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS + 
    FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD
Model 2: SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE + PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + 
    PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_HAWKER_MARKET + 
    PROX_KINDERGARTEN + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + 
    PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET + 
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD
  Res.Df        RSS Df  Sum of Sq      F Pr(>F)
1   1421 8.1206e+14                            
2   1417 8.0947e+14  4 2.5877e+12 1.1325 0.3395


The test gives F = 1.13 with p = 0.34, so removing the four variables as a group costs nothing significant.
The proximity fields are distances, so a negative coefficient means the price falls as the distance grows and buyers pay to be close. Each extra kilometre from the CBD lowers the price by about 77,131, from an MRT station by 294,745 and from a shopping mall by 220,947. Each year of age takes off 24,688, and freehold tenure adds 350,600.
Two positive coefficients surprised me. The price rises by 682,482 for each extra kilometre from a bus stop and by 570,505 for each extra kilometre from a park. Bus stops are close to almost every unit, with a median distance of 0.15 km, so a more useful reading is about 68,000 for every extra 100 m. I checked what the sales farthest from a bus stop look like.


Show the code
condo_region %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(group = if_else(ntile(PROX_BUS_STOP, 10) == 10,
                         "Farthest 10%", "Other 90%")) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(sales = n(),
            median_price = median(SELLING_PRICE),
            median_area = median(AREA_SQM),
            median_units = median(NO_Of_UNITS),
            share_central = mean(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION"))

1 Farthest 10%   143      1650000         140          264         0.538
2 Other 90%     1293      1370000         120          380         0.445


The tenth of sales farthest from a bus stop, 0.31 km or more, have a median price of 1.65 million against 1.37 million for the rest. Their units are bigger (140 against 120 square metres), their developments are smaller (264 against 380 units), and 53.8% of them are in the Central Region against 44.5%. My reading is that PROX_BUS_STOP partly picks up small, low density projects in prime areas whose buyers drive, so the coefficient says more about the type of development than about bus stops.

4.6 Regression diagnostics
Regression diagnostics check whether the model meets the OLS assumptions, which are linear relationships, normal errors with constant variance, no strong multicollinearity and independent observations. The course uses performance for most checks and mentions olsrr, so I ran both where they overlap.

Multicollinearity
check_collinearity() computes the variance inflation factor (VIF) of each variable.


Show the code
check_collinearity(condo.mlr1)


# Check for Multicollinearity

Low Correlation

mlr.vif <- check_collinearity(condo.mlr1)
plot(mlr.vif)









All 14 VIFs are below 3.3. The highest are PROX_CHILDCARE at 3.26 and PROX_BUS_STOP at 2.85, the pair with the 0.77 correlation, and the lowest is AREA_SQM at 1.15. They are far below the usual cut-off of 10, so multicollinearity is not a problem for this model.
ols_vif_tol() of olsrr gives the same VIF and tolerance values.


Show the code
ols_vif_tol(condo.mlr1)

Linearity
check_model() with check = "linearity" plots the residuals against the fitted values. The course text names ols_plot_resid_fit() of olsrr for this step but the code uses performance, so I show both.


Show the code
check_model(condo.mlr1,
            check = "linearity")











Show the code
ols_plot_resid_fit(condo.mlr1)









I read these plots differently from the course page, which concludes that the relationship is linear. Most points do sit around zero, but the reference line in the check_model() plot is curved. It starts above zero for the cheapest predictions, dips slightly below zero in the middle, and climbs steeply after about 4 million. The model underprices both ends of the market, which points to a relationship that is not fully linear, for example floor area being worth more per square metre in prime locations.
The spread of the residuals also grows with the fitted value, a funnel shape that is clearest in the olsrr plot. The leftmost point in both plots has a fitted value below zero.


Show the code
min(fitted(condo.mlr1))


[1] -258526.5


One unit gets a predicted price of -258,527, a reminder that a linear model of raw prices can produce impossible values at the low end.


Normality
check_normality() runs a Shapiro-Wilk test on the standardised residuals.


Show the code
check_normality(condo.mlr1)


Warning: Non-normality of residuals detected (p < .001).


The test rejects normality (p < .001). With 1,436 observations the test reacts to small departures, so the plots matter more than the p-value.


Show the code
plot(check_normality(condo.mlr1),
     type = "qq")











Show the code
check_model(condo.mlr1,
            check = "normality")









The Q-Q plot follows the line through the middle, but the upper tail turns sharply upward from about two standard deviations, and a few points sit far outside the confidence band. The density plot shows the same thing from another side. The residuals are much more peaked than the normal curve and have a long right tail that reaches past 12 million.


Show the code
sum(abs(rstandard(condo.mlr1)) > 3)


[1] 21


21 standardised residuals are beyond ±3, while a normal distribution would give about 4 out of 1,436. The course page describes the residuals as close to normal. That holds for the centre of the distribution, but the tails are much heavier, and the largest errors come from expensive units that the model underprices.
The funnel shape in the linearity plots points to non-constant variance, which performance also tests.


Show the code
check_heteroscedasticity(condo.mlr1)


Warning: Heteroscedasticity (non-constant error variance) detected (p < .001).


The test flags heteroscedasticity (p < .001). The OLS standard errors and p-values above therefore look more precise than they are.


Spatial autocorrelation
The observations are sales at real locations, and nearby sales are likely to share effects that the model does not capture. OLS assumes independent errors, so clustered residuals would make the standard errors and p-values unreliable and would point to a missing locational variable.
I first attach the residuals to the sf data frame. The course also creates mlr.output as a separate data frame, but nothing uses it later, so I skipped it.


Show the code
condo_resale.sf <- cbind(condo_resale.sf,
                         condo.mlr1$residuals) %>%
  rename(`MLR_RES` = `condo.mlr1.residuals`)


The interactive map shows the residuals in ten quantile classes, red for sales the model underpredicts and blue for those it overpredicts.


Show the code
tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(mpsz_view) +
  tm_polygons(fill_alpha = 0.4,
              popup = tm_popup(vars = c("SUBZONE_N", "PLN_AREA_N"))) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +
  tm_symbols(
    fill = "MLR_RES",
    size = 0.7,
    shape = 21,
    col = "black",
    popup = tm_popup(vars = c("SELLING_PRICE", "MLR_RES")),
    fill.scale = tm_scale(
      n = 10,
      values = rev(
        brewer.pal(11, "RdBu")),
      style = "quantile",
      midpoint = NA),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residuals")
  ) +
  tm_title("LM Residuals (Quantile Classification)") +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(11, 14))







Show the code
tmap_mode("plot")








Notetm_dots() has no outline in tmap v4



The course code passes col = "black" to tm_dots() for a black outline. In tmap v4.4 tm_dots() draws a solid dot with no border, so the argument does nothing. I switched to tm_symbols() with shape = 21, which has a fill and an outline, and did the same for the GWR maps in Part 5.


The residuals form patches of the same colour. To check the patches in numbers, I averaged the residuals by planning area.


Show the code
condo_region %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(MLR_RES = condo.mlr1$residuals) %>%
  group_by(PLN_AREA_N) %>%
  summarise(sales = n(),
            mean_residual = mean(MLR_RES)) %>%
  filter(sales >= 15) %>%
  arrange(mean_residual) %>%
  slice(c(1:3, (n() - 2):n()))


# A tibble: 6 × 3
  PLN_AREA_N   sales mean_residual
  <chr>        <int>         <dbl>
1 QUEENSTOWN      41      -643262.
2 JURONG EAST     15      -364843.
3 BISHAN          24      -357955.
4 JURONG WEST     23       662382.
5 RIVER VALLEY    37       733259.
6 NEWTON          27       960696.


Sales in Newton are underpredicted by 960,696 on average, and those in River Valley and Jurong West by more than 660,000. Sales in Queenstown are overpredicted by 643,262, and those in Jurong East and Bishan by more than 350,000. Whole planning areas lean the same way, which is what a missing locational effect looks like.
Global Moran’s I tests this formally. st_dist_band() of sfdep finds all sales within 1,500 m of each sale, and st_weights() turns the neighbour list into row standardised weights.


Show the code
condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>%
  mutate(
    nb = st_dist_band(
      st_geometry(geometry),
      upper = 1500),
    wt = st_weights(
      nb, style = "W"),
    .before = 1)

summary(lengths(condo_resale.sf$nb))


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   1.00   24.00   42.00   46.15   65.00  125.00 


Every sale has at least one neighbour within 1,500 m, and the median sale has 42. global_moran_perm() then runs the permutation test.


Show the code
set.seed(1234)
global_moran_perm(
  condo_resale.sf$MLR_RES,
  nb = condo_resale.sf$nb,
  wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  nsim = 499)



    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  x 
weights: listw  
number of simulations + 1: 500 

statistic = 0.14389, observed rank = 500, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


Moran’s I is 0.144. The observed value ranks 500th out of 500, higher than all 499 permutations, so I reject the null hypothesis that the residuals are randomly distributed. The positive value means that similar residuals cluster together.






TipReading the p-value of a permutation test



The output prints a p-value below 2.2e-16, which looks far more precise than 499 permutations allow. For the two sided test spdep converts the rank of the observed value into a p-value, and a rank at the very top gives exactly zero. With 499 permutations the smallest p-value the test can resolve in one tail is 1 in 500, or 0.002. The conclusion stays the same, since the observed I beat every permutation.

title: Hands-on Ex09: Hedonic Pricing Models with Geographically Weighted Regression
section: Part 5 Hedonic pricing model with GWR
text:
Part 5 Hedonic pricing model with GWR
GWR uses the same 14 variables as condo.mlr1. The bandwidth decides how far each local regression reaches. A fixed bandwidth uses the same distance everywhere, and an adaptive bandwidth uses the same number of nearest neighbours.

5.1 Fixed bandwidth

Computing the bandwidth
bw.gwr() searches for the bandwidth with the best value of a stopping rule. It offers two, cross-validation (approach = "CV") and the corrected Akaike Information Criterion (approach = "AICc"). I follow the course and use CV with a Gaussian kernel, and adaptive = FALSE asks for a fixed distance.


Show the code
bw.fixed <- bw.gwr(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL +
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY +
    FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = FALSE,
  longlat = FALSE)

The search settles on 971.3898 m, the same as the output on the course page. The sentence under that output quotes 971.3405, which looks like a typo.
The bandwidth is in metres because condo_resale.sf uses EPSG 3414, whose unit is the metre, and longlat = FALSE tells GWmodel to compute plain Euclidean distances from the projected coordinates. With longitude and latitude the same call would need longlat = TRUE and would return kilometres.
One step in the search stands out. At 613.79 m the CV score jumps to about 1.38e16, close to 30 times the scores around it. With a kernel that narrow, a sale in a sparse area puts almost all its weight on a handful of neighbours, too few to pin down 15 coefficients, and its leave one out prediction goes far off.


Calibrating the model
gwr.basic() fits the model with the chosen bandwidth and the Gaussian kernel. The output is a list of class gwrm.

    FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  bw = bw.fixed,
  kernel = "gaussian",
  longlat = FALSE)

The effective number of parameters is 438.4, against 15 for OLS.
The coefficient summary shows how far the local estimates swing. The median AREA_SQM coefficient is 7,474, below the global 12,778, and the local values run from 1,000 to 21,575. Some ranges are hard to believe. The intercept goes from -36 million to 113 million, and the PROX_CBD coefficient reaches -77 million per kilometre. Section 6.5 traces where these values come from.



5.2 Adaptive bandwidth

Computing the bandwidth
An adaptive bandwidth uses a fixed number of nearest neighbours at each sale, so the kernel widens where sales are sparse and narrows where they are dense. The call is the same as before except for adaptive = TRUE.


Show the code
bw.adaptive <- bw.gwr(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL +
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS +
    FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)

The adaptive model has an AICc of 41,982.22, about 281 below the fixed model, with fewer effective parameters, 350.3 against 438.4. R² is almost the same at 0.891, and adjusted R² rises to 0.856 because the model uses up fewer degrees of freedom.
Most coefficient ranges are narrower than in the fixed model, but a few get wider. The PROX_MRT coefficient drops to -43.8 million and PROX_SHOPPING_MALL reaches 38.0 million. Section 6.5 shows that both come from a single sale.



5.3 What the GWR output holds
The SDF element of the result holds one row per sale. It has the local coefficients, the observed y, the fitted yhat, the residual, the studentised residual, the standard error of each coefficient (_SE), its pseudo t-value (_TV) and the local R².
Each field answers a different question. Local R² runs from 0 to 1 and shows how well the local model fits the sales around a point, so a map of it shows where the model works and where a variable might be missing. The standard errors show how reliable each local coefficient is. A coefficient deserves more trust when its standard error is small next to its value, and large standard errors can be a sign of local collinearity. The standardised residuals have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one, and a cold to hot map of them shows where the model over or under predicts.
The course notes also describe a condition number, where values above 30 point to unstable results from local collinearity. gwr.basic() does not return that field. GWmodel computes local collinearity diagnostics in a separate function, gwr.collin.diagno().


5.4 Converting SDF into an sf data frame
st_as_sf() converts SDF into an sf data frame, and st_transform() makes sure it is in EPSG 3414.

Local R² is high almost everywhere. It runs from 0.672 to 0.993 with a median of 0.907, and only 12 sales fall below 0.7.
The pattern on the map surprised me. I expected the dense central area to fit best because it has the most data, and the opposite happened. 6.1 Modelling log price

The criterion matters little for the Gaussian kernel. AICc picks 27 neighbours instead of 30, and the model’s AICc drops by only 3.6.
The kernel matters much more. With a bisquare kernel the search picks 93 neighbours by CV and 84 by AICc, and the AICc falls to 41,745.32 and 41,712.41, about 240 to 270 below the Gaussian models. R² rises to 0.926 and 0.933.
The two kernels count neighbours differently. A bisquare window of 84 neighbours gives zero weight to everything beyond the 84th sale, while a Gaussian window of 30 gives every sale on the island some weight, and the 30th neighbour only marks where the weight has dropped to about 0.61. The bisquare model ends up more local, which the effective number of parameters confirms, 469 against 350.
I keep the Gaussian adaptive model as the main model to stay in line with the course, but on AICc the bisquare kernel fits these data better. Its 469 effective parameters are about a third of the sample size, which makes me careful about reading single local coefficients from it.

The OLS value of 12,778 sits close to the Central figure, because the Central Region holds 653 of the 1,436 sales and most of the expensive ones.
Age and tenure follow the same pattern. A year of age costs a median of 33,489 in the Central Region against 3,853 in the West, and the freehold premium is 375,892 in the centre against 65,504 in the West.

title: Hands-on Ex09: Hedonic Pricing Models with Geographically Weighted Regression
text:
My takeaway
The OLS model explained 65% of the variation in condominium prices, and its residuals were clustered in space with Moran’s I of 0.144. Whole planning areas leaned the same way, with Newton underpredicted by close to a million on average and Queenstown overpredicted by more than 600,000. GWR with an adaptive Gaussian bandwidth of 30 neighbours raised R² to 0.891, lowered AICc by 985 and removed the positive clustering.
The local coefficients showed that one global model mixes very different markets. An extra square metre is worth about 13,300 in the Central Region and 5,300 to 7,000 elsewhere, and distance to an MRT station lowers the price mainly in the centre. PROX_CHILDCARE and PROX_PRIMARY_SCH were significant in OLS but are significant at less than a quarter of the sales locally.
The extreme coefficients taught me to read every GWR coefficient map with its t-values next to it. The largest values came from Sentosa under the fixed bandwidth and from tight clusters under the adaptive one, wherever a distance variable barely changes inside the window.
The diagnostics also changed how I see the course model. The OLS residuals have heavy tails and non-constant variance, and the log price model fixed most of the non-normality but made the residual clustering stronger (I = 0.200). A bisquare kernel lowered AICc by another 270. A GWR on log price with a bisquare kernel is the combination I would test next.
